title: Habitats: the places that give living things what they need

summary.text: This unit is about habitats. A habitat is the place where a living thing finds everything it needs: food, water, air, shelter, space and the right warmth. A pond, a forest, a desert and the sea are four very different habitats. Each one gives some things easily and makes other things hard. Even tiny places, like the space under a stone, are habitats with their own weather. Living things do not just sit in their habitats. They change them too: trees make shade and damp air, and worms make soil. Your own body is a habitat for trillions of tiny living things. Scientists still argue about where one habitat ends and the next begins, and nobody knows yet if any other world has a habitat with life.
summary.art: Four windows in one wall: a pond with a lotus and a frog, a forest with a hornbill, a desert with a camel and a khejri tree, and the blue sea with a turtle; in the corner, a magnifying glass over a stone with a beetle underneath.

intro.hook: Find a stone or a flowerpot in a garden, a park or a balcony. Do not lift it yet. Guess first: how many living things are hiding under it? Now lift it gently and count.
intro.text: In February 1977, a pilot and two scientists squeezed into a tiny submarine called Alvin. They sank more than two kilometres down into the dark Pacific Ocean, near the Galapagos Islands. No sunlight ever reaches that deep. They expected bare rock, cold and empty, like a desert. Instead, around cracks in the sea floor where hot water gushed out, they found a crowd. There were giant red-tipped worms longer than a grown-up is tall. There were clams as big as dinner plates, and pale crabs. How could so much life live where there is no sunlight and no plants? What was that place giving them? This unit is about habitats: the places that give living things what they need.
intro.art: A small white submarine with its lights on, deep in black water, lighting up a crowd of tall white tube worms with red tips, big clams and pale crabs around a smoking crack in the rock.

outcomes: I can say what a habitat is, and name the things it gives a living thing: food, water, air, shelter, space and the right warmth.
I can compare a pond, a forest, a desert and the sea: what each one gives easily, and what is hard about living there.
I can find small habitats near my home, like under a stone, and show with a fair test that small places can be very different.
I can explain that the living and non-living parts of a habitat depend on each other, and that living things change their habitats.
I can say how people destroy habitats and how people make and protect them, with real examples from India.
I can say what scientists agree about habitats, and what they still do not know, such as where a habitat ends and whether life lives on other worlds.
I can explain that my own body is a habitat, and go from a stone in the garden out to the deep sea, deep rock and other planets.

terms.meaning: The place where a living thing lives and finds everything it needs to stay alive.
terms.example: A pond is the habitat of a frog. It finds water, insects to eat and mud to hide in.
terms.art: A frog on a lily pad with small labels pointing to water, an insect and mud.

terms.meaning: The things a living thing must have to stay alive and grow. Most need food, water, air, shelter, space and the right warmth.
terms.example: You need food, water and air every day. You need a home to keep you safe from rain and sun.
terms.art: Six small picture icons in a circle: a leaf for food, a drop for water, a swirl for air, a roof for shelter, open arms for space, a sun and snowflake for warmth.

terms.meaning: A safe place to rest, hide or sleep, away from hot sun, rain, cold and hungry animals.
terms.example: A tree hollow is a shelter for an owl. A burrow is a shelter for a desert rat.
terms.art: An owl peeping out of a hollow in a tree trunk.

terms.meaning: A small, still body of fresh water. Fresh water is water that is not salty.
terms.example: The pond in a village has frogs, fish, snails, dragonflies and lotus plants.
terms.art: A village pond with lotus leaves, a frog, a dragonfly and a buffalo cooling off at the edge.

terms.meaning: A large place covered with many trees growing close together, with plants and animals living at every level.
terms.example: The Western Ghats have thick forests where hornbills, monkeys and frogs live.
terms.art: A tall forest drawn in layers, with a hornbill at the top, a monkey in the middle and a frog on the leafy floor.

terms.meaning: A place that gets very little rain all year. Deserts can be hot, like the Thar, or cold, like Ladakh.
terms.example: In the Thar Desert in Rajasthan, camels, desert foxes and khejri trees live with very little water.
terms.art: Sand dunes with a camel, a desert fox at a burrow and a khejri tree.

terms.meaning: The huge body of salty water that covers most of the Earth. The biggest seas are called oceans.
terms.example: Fish, turtles, crabs, dolphins and corals live in the sea around India.
terms.art: A cut-away view of the sea from the bright top to the dark bottom, with a turtle, fish and a crab.

terms.meaning: A very small habitat inside a bigger one. Micro means very small.
terms.example: The damp space under a stone in a garden is a microhabitat for woodlice and worms.
terms.art: A lifted stone with woodlice, a worm and an ant underneath, inside a bigger picture of a garden.

terms.meaning: The parts of a habitat that are alive: plants, animals, fungi and tiny living things too small to see.
terms.example: In a forest, the trees, birds, mushrooms and ants are living parts.
terms.art: A forest scene with only the living things coloured in.

terms.meaning: The parts of a habitat that are not alive, but that living things need: sunlight, water, air, soil, rocks and warmth.
terms.example: In a desert, the sand, the hot sun and the rare rain are non-living parts.
terms.art: The same forest scene with only the sun, rain, rocks, soil and air coloured in.

terms.meaning: A small grey creature with seven pairs of legs that lives in damp, dark places. Some kinds roll into a ball. It is not an insect. It is a cousin of crabs and prawns.
terms.example: You often find woodlice under flowerpots and fallen leaves.
terms.art: A grey woodlouse walking and another rolled into a ball, with a crab drawn faintly behind as a cousin.

terms.meaning: The top layer of a forest, where the branches and leaves of the tall trees meet like a roof.
terms.example: Hornbills and many monkeys live high in the canopy.
terms.art: A forest from below, with the leafy canopy like a green roof and light coming through.

terms.meaning: A kind of tree that grows in salty mud where rivers meet the sea. Its roots stand up out of the mud.
terms.example: The Sundarbans in West Bengal is the biggest mangrove forest in the world.
terms.art: Mangrove trees standing on tangled roots in muddy water, with a crab on a root.

terms.meaning: A habitat in warm, shallow sea made by tiny animals called corals. They build hard homes that join into a huge reef.
terms.example: There are coral reefs around the Andaman and Nicobar Islands and in the Gulf of Mannar.
terms.art: A colourful coral reef with small fish swimming among the corals.

terms.meaning: How hot or cold something is. We measure it in degrees Celsius with a thermometer.
terms.example: A sunny path at noon can be over 40 degrees Celsius. The ground under a stone may be about 30.
terms.art: A thermometer stuck in sunny soil next to one under a stone, showing two different readings.

terms.meaning: A test where you change only one thing and keep everything else the same, so you know what made the difference.
terms.example: To test whether woodlice like damp or dry, change only the dampness. Keep the light the same on both sides.
terms.art: Two halves of a tray, one damp and one dry, with a sign saying 'only this is different'.

terms.meaning: When a habitat is destroyed or changed so much that its living things can no longer live there.
terms.example: When a pond is filled in to build houses, the frogs and fish lose their habitat.
terms.art: A pond half-covered by a pile of sand and bricks, with frogs hopping away.

terms.meaning: How many different kinds of living things there are in a place. Bio means life.
terms.example: A forest in the Western Ghats has a huge biodiversity: thousands of kinds of plants and animals.
terms.art: A crowded patch of forest floor with many different small plants, insects and a frog.

terms.meaning: A crack in the deep sea floor where very hot water full of minerals gushes out. Strange animals live around it.
terms.example: Giant tube worms live around hydrothermal vents, in the dark, more than two kilometres down.
terms.art: A chimney of rock on the dark sea floor puffing black water, with tube worms around it.

terms.meaning: A living thing so small that you can only see it through a microscope. Bacteria are microbes.
terms.example: Microbes in milk turn it into curd. Microbes on your skin and in your tummy live with you all the time.
terms.art: A drop of curd under a magnifying glass with tiny friendly rod-shaped bacteria.

explanations.definition: A habitat is the place where a living thing lives and finds everything it needs to stay alive: food, water, air, shelter, space and the right warmth.
explanations.description: A habitat is a place that gives something. A crow lives in a town because the town gives it scraps to eat, water in tanks and drains, trees and ledges to nest on, and room to fly. If one of these goes, the crow must move or it dies. So when you want to know if a place is a habitat for an animal, ask six questions. Is there food? Is there water? Is there air? Is there shelter? Is there enough space? Is it the right warmth? Plants need things too: sunlight, water, air, soil and space for their roots.
examples: A fish's habitat is water. It gets food, oxygen from the water and places to hide among water plants.
A house sparrow's habitat is near people. It eats grain and insects, and nests in holes in walls and roofs.
A cactus's habitat is the dry desert. It gets plenty of sunlight, and it stores the little rain that falls.
explanations.art: A crow on a wire above a town street, with small labels pointing to a dustbin (food), a water tank (water), a tree with a nest (shelter) and the open sky (space).
explanations.context: This card explains the main idea of the whole unit: what a habitat is.

explanations.concept: Living and non-living parts work together
explanations.definition: A habitat has living parts, such as plants, animals and microbes, and non-living parts, such as sunlight, water, air, soil and rocks. Each kind changes the other.
explanations.description: Every habitat has living parts, like plants, animals and microbes. It also has non-living parts, like sunlight, water, air, rocks, soil and warmth. The two kinds are not separate. They change each other all the time. Rain makes a pond. The pond lets lotus plants grow. The plants make oxygen, which the fish breathe. Dead leaves fall and rot, and this makes the mud richer. So a habitat is not a box with animals inside it. It is a living system where everything affects everything else.
examples: In a forest, trees give shade. The shade keeps the soil damp, so worms and frogs can live there.
Earthworms eat dead leaves and mix them into the soil. This makes the soil better for plants.
In a desert, the rare rain makes seeds that have waited in the sand for months sprout in a few days.
explanations.art: A pond drawn as a circle of arrows: rain fills the pond, the lotus grows, a fish breathes, a leaf falls and rots into mud, the mud feeds the lotus.
explanations.context: A habitat has living parts and non-living parts. This card shows how they work together.

explanations.concept: The pond: a home made of fresh water
explanations.definition: A pond is a small, still body of fresh water. It is a habitat for living things that need to stay wet or live in water.
explanations.description: A pond is a small, still pool of fresh water. Fresh water is water that is not salty. A pond gives water all the time, so it is a habitat for things that must stay wet, like fish, tadpoles and water snails. It gives food: tiny green algae, water plants, insects and worms. It gives shelter in the mud at the bottom and among the plants. Life in a pond lives at different levels. Some things float on top, like duckweed and water striders. Some swim in the middle, like fish. Some live in the mud, like worms and snails. What is hard about a pond? In summer, a small pond can dry up. Some frogs and fish then bury themselves in the mud and wait for rain.
examples: A lotus roots in the mud, but its leaves float on top to catch sunlight.
A water strider is an insect that walks on top of the water without sinking.
Some tiny pond animals lay eggs that can lie in dry mud for years, then hatch when the rain comes back.
explanations.art: A cut-away pond showing three levels: a water strider and duckweed on top, fish and tadpoles in the middle, snails and worms in the mud at the bottom.
explanations.context: This card is about the pond, one of the four big habitats in this unit, and what it gives the living things there.

explanations.concept: The forest: homes at every level
explanations.definition: A forest is a large area of trees growing close together, with different homes at each level, from the canopy at the top to the forest floor.
explanations.description: A forest is a place with many trees growing close together. Trees make a forest a habitat at many levels, like a tall building with many floors. At the very top is the canopy, where leaves catch most of the sunlight. Hornbills, monkeys and many insects live there. In the middle are smaller trees and climbers. On the dark, damp forest floor, fallen leaves rot into soil. Worms, beetles, frogs, fungi and snakes live there. A forest gives food all year, because different trees flower and fruit at different times. It gives shelter in hollows, under bark and under leaves. It also gives shade and damp air. What is hard about a forest? On the floor, there is very little sunlight, so small plants must find ways to reach the light.
examples: A tailorbird stitches leaves together with plant threads to make its nest.
An owl rests by day in a tree hollow and hunts at night.
The Western Ghats forests are home to thousands of kinds of plants and animals. Many live nowhere else on Earth.
explanations.art: A tall forest drawn like a building with floors: hornbills and monkeys in the canopy, a tailorbird's leaf nest in the middle, a frog, beetle and mushrooms on the dark floor.
explanations.context: This card is about the forest, one of the four big habitats in this unit, and the homes it has at every level.

explanations.concept: The desert: little water, lots of life
explanations.definition: A desert is a place that gets very little rain all year. It can be hot or cold.
explanations.description: A desert is a place that gets very little rain. People often think a desert is empty. It is not. The Thar Desert in Rajasthan is home to camels, desert foxes, chinkara deer, lizards, snakes, beetles and birds like the great Indian bustard. A desert gives plenty of sunlight and lots of open space. What is hard is water, and heat. Days can be burning hot and nights can be cold. So many desert animals stay hidden in burrows by day and come out at night or at dawn. Some get almost all their water from the food they eat. Desert plants have deep roots, small leaves or thick stems that store water. Not every desert is hot. Ladakh is a cold desert, high in the mountains, where it hardly rains and winters are freezing.
examples: The khejri tree's roots go very deep to reach water far under the sand.
The desert fox shelters in a cool burrow by day and hunts at night.
After a rare shower, the desert can turn green with new plants in a few days.
explanations.art: A desert at noon and the same desert at night: empty-looking sand by day with a burrow entrance; at night, a fox, a lizard, beetles and a jerboa out under the stars.
explanations.context: This card is about the desert, one of the four big habitats in this unit. It explains why a desert is not empty.

explanations.concept: The sea: the biggest habitat on Earth
explanations.definition: The sea is the huge body of salty water that covers most of the Earth. Its biggest parts are called oceans.
explanations.description: The sea is salty water that covers about seven parts out of every ten of the Earth's surface. It is so deep that most of the space where life can live on our planet is under the sea. Near the top, where sunlight reaches, tiny floating plant-like living things called phytoplankton make food from sunlight. Fish, turtles, dolphins and whales live here. Along the coast, there are rocky shores, sandy beaches, coral reefs and mangrove forests. Deeper down, it gets darker, colder and the water presses harder. At the bottom, in total darkness, live strange fish, worms and crabs. What is hard about the sea? Salt, waves, darkness in the deep and cold.
examples: Olive ridley turtles come in huge numbers to lay eggs on beaches in Odisha.
Corals around the Andaman Islands build reefs that give homes to hundreds of kinds of fish.
In the Sundarbans mangroves, tigers swim between muddy islands, and crabs climb the roots.
explanations.art: A tall cut-away of the sea: a turtle and fish in the bright top, a dolphin lower down, a glowing fish in the dark middle and crabs and worms on the black bottom.
explanations.context: This card is about the sea, the biggest of the four habitats in this unit, and the different places to live inside it.

explanations.definition: Every habitat gives some needs easily and makes others hard to meet. Living things live where they can use what the place gives.
explanations.description: Every habitat gives some things easily and makes other things hard. That is why different living things live in each one. Look at the table. A pond always has water but can dry up in summer. A forest has food and shelter but little light on the floor. A desert has lots of sun and space but little water. The sea has water everywhere, but it is salty, and deep down it is dark and cold. No habitat gives everything. Each living thing fits the place whose gifts it can use, and whose problems it can handle.
examples: A camel can go days without drinking, so the desert suits it. It would not manage in a pond.
A frog's skin must stay wet, so it lives near ponds, not in the open desert.
A sea fish needs salty water. Most pond fish would die in the sea.
explanations.art: Four columns with an icon at the top of each (pond, forest, desert, sea), and a green tick or a red cross next to water, food, shelter, light and warmth.
explanations.context: We have met four habitats: pond, forest, desert and sea. This card compares what each one gives easily and what is hard there.

explanations.concept: Microhabitats: small worlds in small places
explanations.definition: A microhabitat is a very small habitat inside a bigger habitat, with its own conditions of light, warmth and dampness.
explanations.description: A microhabitat is a very small habitat inside a bigger one. The space under a stone is one. So is a crack in a wall, the underside of a leaf, a puddle or a rotting log. Each small place has its own weather. Under a stone it is darker, cooler and damper than on the open path next to it. That is why woodlice, worms, centipedes and ants live there and not on the hot path. You do not need to travel to a forest to study habitats. You can find ten microhabitats in one garden, one park or one balcony.
examples: A rotting log is a microhabitat for beetles, termites and fungi.
A crack in a damp wall is a microhabitat for moss, spiders and geckos.
Even one leaf can be a microhabitat for aphids and the ladybirds that eat them.
explanations.art: A garden drawn with circles zooming into five small places: under a stone, a crack in a wall, the back of a leaf, a puddle and a rotting log, each with its tiny residents.
explanations.context: A habitat can be as small as the space under a stone. This card explains microhabitats.

explanations.definition: Living things do not just live in their habitats. They change them, for example by making shade, soil, damp air or reefs.
explanations.description: We often say an animal lives in a habitat, as if the habitat were a box. But living things change their habitats all the time. Trees make shade and drop leaves that become soil. Their leaves breathe out water into the air, so a forest stays damp, and the forest helps make its own rain. Earthworms and ants dig and mix the soil. Corals build whole reefs that thousands of other creatures then live in. Beavers in some countries build dams that turn a stream into a pond. People change habitats more than any other living thing. So a habitat and its living things make each other.
examples: Over a large forest like the Amazon, a big share of the rain is water that the forest's own leaves gave off.
Termites build tall mounds of mud that change the soil around them for years.
Elephants knock over small trees and open up grassland, which helps deer and other grazers.
explanations.art: A bare sandbar turning, in four small pictures, into a forest: grass, then bamboo, then trees with birds, then a forest with a rain cloud above it.
explanations.context: This card explains that living things are not just inside their habitats. They change and even make them.

explanations.concept: People destroy habitats, and people make them
explanations.definition: Habitat loss is when a habitat is destroyed or changed so much that its living things can no longer live there. People can also protect and restore habitats.
explanations.description: Scientists agree that the biggest danger to wild plants and animals today is losing their habitats. People cut forests for farms, roads and towns. They fill in ponds and wetlands, and dirty rivers and seas. When the habitat goes, the living things go with it. The great Indian bustard, a tall bird of the Thar grasslands, is now very rare, partly because its open grasslands have been turned into farms and crossed by power lines. But people also protect and make habitats. In 1974, in the village of Reni in the Himalaya, Gaura Devi and the women of the village hugged their trees to stop them being cut. This was part of the Chipko movement. In Assam, Jadav Payeng planted a forest on a bare sandbar, starting in 1979. Elephants, deer and birds now live in it.
examples: People in Kerala, led by many groups and the poet Sugathakumari, protested to save the Silent Valley forest from being flooded by a dam. It became a national park in 1984.
Many villages in India keep sacred groves: patches of forest where no tree is cut. They are some of the oldest forests left.
A clay bowl of water on a balcony can make a small habitat for birds and insects in summer.
explanations.art: Two halves: on the left a forest being cut for a road; on the right women with their arms around tree trunks, and a young man planting bamboo on a sandbar.
explanations.context: This card is about how people harm habitats, and how people have protected and even made them.

explanations.definition: Your body is a habitat for microbes: tiny living things, mostly bacteria, that live on your skin and inside you.
explanations.description: You live in habitats. But you are also a habitat. Tiny living things called microbes live on your skin, in your mouth and most of all in your tummy. Scientists have counted them. A grown-up's body has about as many bacteria living in it as it has human cells. Most of them are harmless or helpful. The ones in your tummy help you break down food and help protect you from germs. Your body gives them food, water, warmth and shelter, just like a pond gives a frog. Most grown-ups even have tiny mites living in the roots of their eyelashes and face hairs. They are too small to see and do no harm.
examples: Curd is made by bacteria. Warm milk is a good habitat for them, so they grow and turn it into curd.
Your skin is drier on your arms and damper in your armpits. Different microbes live in each place, like different animals in a desert and a pond.
When a baby is born, it picks up its first microbes from its mother and the world around it.
explanations.art: A child's outline with zoom-in circles on the skin, the mouth and the tummy, each showing friendly round and rod-shaped microbes.
explanations.context: We usually think of habitats as places like ponds and forests. This card explains that your own body is a habitat too.

explanations.concept: Habitats at the edge: is there anywhere life cannot live?
explanations.description: Scientists keep finding life in places that once seemed impossible. Around hydrothermal vents on the deep sea floor, there is no sunlight at all. There, bacteria make food from chemicals in the hot water, not from light. Worms, clams and crabs live off these bacteria. In 1969, Thomas Brock and Hudson Freeze found bacteria living in springs hotter than a cup of tea in Yellowstone, in the United States. Bacteria have been found living about three kilometres down inside the rock, in a gold mine in South Africa. Tiny animals called tardigrades, or water bears, live in moss and can survive being dried out for years. So scientists now think life can live almost anywhere there is liquid water and some kind of energy. But nobody knows exactly where the limits are.
examples: Tube worms near deep sea vents have no mouth. Bacteria living inside their bodies make their food.
Tardigrades live in the moss on walls and trees, maybe even near your home.
Some microbes live inside the ice of Antarctica.
explanations.art: A strip of extreme homes: a tube worm at a black smoker, a steaming hot spring, a deep mine tunnel with glowing microbes, a tardigrade in moss and an icy Antarctic lake.
explanations.context: Life lives in ponds, forests, deserts and seas. This card is about stranger places, and the idea that life can live almost anywhere with water and energy.

explanations.description: So far, Earth is the only place in the whole universe where we know for sure that life lives. Scientists are now asking: does any other world give what life needs? The big clue they look for is liquid water, plus energy and the right chemicals. Mars once had rivers and lakes, and may still have water frozen under its ground. Europa, a moon of Jupiter, and Enceladus, a moon of Saturn, have oceans of salty water hidden under thick ice. In 2005, the Cassini spacecraft saw jets of water shooting out of Enceladus into space. Could there be living things there, like the life at deep sea vents? Nobody knows yet. This is one of the biggest questions in science.
examples: Rovers on Mars are searching rocks for signs of tiny life from long ago.
Scientists call the region around a star where a planet could have liquid water the habitable zone.
Thousands of planets have now been found circling other stars. Some are in their star's habitable zone.
explanations.art: The Earth, Mars, the icy moon Enceladus with water jets spraying into space, and a far-off planet circling another star, each with a question mark.
explanations.context: We have looked at habitats on Earth. This card asks whether there are any habitats for life on other worlds, which nobody knows yet.

explanations.description: On a map, we draw a neat line between a forest and a grassland, or between a pond and the land. In real life, it is usually not neat. Near the edge of a forest, trees slowly thin out. Near a pond, the ground gets wetter step by step. Scientists have argued for over a hundred years about whether habitats are real things with edges, or just names we give to parts of one big, changing world.
examples: The muddy edge of a pond is part pond and part land. Frogs live in both.
Where a river meets the sea, the water is part fresh and part salty. Mangroves grow there.

perspectives.who: Frederic Clements, an American plant scientist, in 1916
perspectives.explanation: The plants in a place grow together like one big living thing, almost like a body. So a forest or a grassland is a real unit with a clear place where it ends.

perspectives.who: Henry Gleason, an American plant scientist, in 1926
perspectives.explanation: Each kind of plant grows wherever the conditions suit it, on its own. Plants do not move together in teams. So habitats blend into each other with no real edges. Most scientists ignored him for about thirty years. Later, careful counts of plants along slopes showed he was largely right.

Both ideas help. Each kind of living thing does spread out on its own, as Gleason said. But some places do have fairly sharp edges, like where a forest meets a lake, or where a river bank drops. Naming habitats is useful, as long as we remember that nature does not draw the lines.

explanations.art: A pond edge drawn as a smooth fade from deep water to shallow, to mud, to wet grass, to dry ground, with a question mark where the line should be.
explanations.context: We draw neat lines between habitats on maps. This card is about a real argument among scientists: do habitats really have edges?

explanations.concept: Should people live inside wild habitats?
explanations.description: To protect a habitat, should we keep people out of it, or should we let the people who have always lived there look after it? This is a real argument, in India and around the world.
examples: The Bishnoi people of Rajasthan have protected khejri trees and blackbuck deer for hundreds of years.
Some tiger reserves have moved villages out, so that tigers have more space.

perspectives.who: Many wildlife scientists and park managers
perspectives.explanation: Some animals, like tigers and elephants, need very large areas with few people. Farms, roads and cattle inside a forest can slowly break it up. So some places need to be kept mostly free of people.

perspectives.who: Many forest communities, and scientists like Madhav Gadgil, an Indian ecologist who studied sacred groves
perspectives.explanation: Local people often know a forest best and have cared for it for generations. Sacred groves and Bishnoi villages show this. Moving people out can be unfair to them, and can even leave a forest with no one to protect it.
It depends on the place and the animals. In many places, the best results come when local people share in decisions and in the benefits of protecting the habitat.

explanations.art: A forest with a fence around it on one side, and on the other side a village family walking a path inside a forest, collecting fallen leaves.
explanations.context: This card is about a real argument: is it better to protect wild places by keeping people out, or by letting local people care for them?

agreed.text: Every living thing needs a habitat that gives it food, water, air, shelter, space and the right warmth.
agreed.evidence: When scientists keep animals or plants in a place without one of these, they do not survive. When a habitat loses one of them, its animals move away or die.

agreed.text: Different habitats have different living things, because each habitat gives different things easily.
agreed.evidence: Scientists have counted plants and animals in habitats all over the world for more than two hundred years. The same kinds of habitat, like deserts, have similar kinds of life, even on different continents.

agreed.text: Even small places, like under a stone, are habitats with their own conditions.
agreed.evidence: Thermometers and moisture meters show that under a stone, it is cooler and damper than on the open ground just next to it. Woodlice and worms choose those places in tests.

agreed.text: Living things change their habitats, and the habitat changes them back.
agreed.evidence: Measurements show forests keep the air damp and help make rain. Earthworms measurably mix soil, as Charles Darwin showed in 1881.

agreed.text: Habitat loss is the biggest danger to wild plants and animals today.
agreed.evidence: A large study by hundreds of scientists for the United Nations, published in 2019, found that changing land and sea for human use is the main cause of the loss of wild species.

challenging.claim: Deserts and the deep sea are empty places with almost no life.
challenging.who: A common belief. Many scientists thought the deep sea floor was nearly lifeless until the 1970s.
challenging.for: In the day, a desert looks bare. The deep sea is dark and cold, with no plants.
challenging.against: Desert animals hide by day and come out at night. In 1977, scientists in the submarine Alvin found crowds of worms, clams and crabs around hot vents more than two kilometres down. Empty-looking is not the same as empty.
challenging.context: This card is about a common idea that some habitats are empty, and why scientists gave it up.

challenging.claim: A habitat is just a place, like a box that animals live in.
challenging.who: A common way of talking, and how many textbooks draw habitats.
challenging.for: We can point to a pond on a map. It seems to be there before any frog moves in.
challenging.against: Living things build and change their habitats. Corals build reefs. Trees make shade, soil and damp air. A sandbar became a forest because plants and animals changed it. So the place and its life make each other.
challenging.context: This card questions the usual way we think about habitats: as boxes that living things simply sit inside.

challenging.claim: Every place has one clear habitat, with a sharp edge.
challenging.who: Frederic Clements, a plant scientist, in 1916, and the way maps are drawn
challenging.for: Some edges are sharp, like where a lake meets a cliff.
challenging.against: Henry Gleason, in 1926, showed that plants spread out one kind at a time, and most habitats blend into each other. Most scientists now agree habitats usually fade into each other.
challenging.context: This card is about whether habitats have sharp edges, an argument scientists have had for over a hundred years.

challenging.claim: Zoos and aquariums can be real habitats for wild animals.
challenging.who: Some zoo keepers, and many visitors
challenging.for: Good zoos give animals food, water, shelter and medical care. Some rare animals survive only because they are bred in zoos.
challenging.against: A zoo cannot give the space many animals need. An elephant may walk many kilometres a day in the wild. Many scientists say the best way to save an animal is to save its wild habitat.
challenging.context: This card is about a real argument: can a zoo give an animal everything its wild habitat gives?

challenging.for: Almost all food chains on Earth start with plants, which need sunlight to make food.
challenging.against: At deep sea vents, and deep inside rocks, bacteria make food from chemicals, with no sunlight at all. Whole communities live on them.
challenging.context: This card is about an old idea, that all life needs sunlight, and the discovery that proved it wrong.

big_questions.q: Is there any place on Earth where nothing at all lives?
big_questions.hint: Scientists keep finding life in very hot springs, deep rock and Antarctic ice. What would a place need to lack for nothing to live there?

big_questions.q: If your body is a habitat for trillions of microbes, are they part of you, or are they guests?
big_questions.hint: Some of them help you digest food. You could not live well without them.

big_questions.q: Where does a pond end and the land begin?
big_questions.hint: Walk slowly from deep water to dry ground. Where would you draw the line? Would a frog agree?

big_questions.q: Why does a desert look empty in the daytime?
big_questions.hint: Where would you go if you were a small animal on hot sand at noon?

big_questions.q: Do people have a habitat? What does yours give you?
big_questions.hint: Think about your food, water, shelter and space. Where do they really come from?

big_questions.q: Who owns a forest: the people, the government, or the animals who live there?
big_questions.hint: Think about the Bishnoi, the women of Reni, and the hornbill nesting in a tree.

big_questions.q: If you could choose any habitat in this unit to live in as an animal, which would you choose, and what would be hard for you there?
big_questions.hint: Every habitat gives some things easily and makes other things hard.

big_questions.q: Could there be living things in the ocean under the ice of Enceladus, a moon of Saturn?
big_questions.hint: Remember the deep sea vents, where life lives with no sunlight.

big_questions.q: Is a city a habitat? For whom?
big_questions.hint: Think of crows, pigeons, rats, geckos and the microbes in drains.

big_questions.q: When a habitat is destroyed, where do its animals go?
big_questions.hint: Some move. Some cannot. What happens when there is nowhere left to move to?

big_questions.q: Do the microbes in curd know they are living in milk?
big_questions.hint: What does it mean for a living thing to fit its habitat without knowing anything about it?

story.title: What the Sandbar Learned to Give
story.note: Jadav Payeng is real. He began planting on a bare sandbar of the Brahmaputra in 1979, when he was about sixteen, after a flood. The dead snakes on the shadeless sandbar, the bamboo, the red ants he carried from his village, and the elephants, deer, rhinos and tigers that came later are all from his own accounts and from news reports. The forest is now called the Molai forest, after his nickname. The river's voice, the old man's words, what Jadav said and the small details of each day are imagined.
text: I am the river Brahmaputra. I come down from the snow, wide and brown, and I cross Assam on my way to the sea. Every monsoon, the rain fills me and I grow strong. I carry sand and mud with me, and I drop them in heaps in the middle of my water. These heaps are islands of sand, called sandbars. People here call them chapori. I make them, and I take them away again. I have done this for longer than anyone can remember.

In 1979, after a great flood, I left one of my sandbars bare. It lay near Majuli, the big river island. When my water went down, the sun came out hard. There was no tree on that sandbar. There was no bush. There was no grass. There was only hot sand, shining white, and nowhere for anything to hide.

Snakes had come down with my flood, clinging to logs and roots. They crawled up onto the sandbar to dry. A snake cannot make its own cool. It needs the world to give it shade when the sun is fierce. That day, the sandbar gave nothing. By afternoon, many of the snakes lay dead in the sand, dry and still.

A boy found them. His name was Jadav. He was about sixteen years old, and people called him Molai. He walked among the snakes for a long time. I have watched many people look at my floods and blame me. Jadav did not blame me. He crouched down and pressed his palm on the sand. Then he pulled it back fast.
"They didn't drown," he said, to nobody. "They cooked."

He went to the old people of his village. "What can I do?" he asked. "Can I carry the snakes somewhere cool?" An old man shook his head. "You cannot carry every snake," he said. "Tomorrow there will be more. Don't carry the animals to a home. Make a home, and the animals will come."
"Grow trees," said the old man. "Start with bamboo. Bamboo is stubborn."

So Jadav came back to my sandbar with a bundle of bamboo plants. I laughed, the way a river laughs, with a small wave against the sand. Sandbars are mine. I make them and I unmake them. What were a few little plants against me?

But he came back the next day, and the next. The sand let water run straight through it, so the young plants were always thirsty. He carried my own water up from the edge in pots. He dug. He planted. Some plants died. He planted again. Other boys went to school, or to the fields, or into town. Jadav went to the sandbar.

The bamboo grew. Where there had been white sand, there was now a strip of green shade. In the next hot season, something small happened. A lizard lay in that shade at noon. A snake curled under the leaves. A spider strung a web between two stalks. Nobody had carried them there. The shade had called them.

Then Jadav did something the village laughed at. He went home and filled a bag with red ants from the trees near his house. He carried them all the way to the sandbar, while they bit his arms, and let them go. "This sand is dead," he told his family. "The ants will wake it up."

Ants dig. They carry bits of leaf underground. They mix the sand with dead things. Slowly, very slowly, my sand began to turn into soil. Now other trees could grow, trees that needed more than sand. Jadav planted those too, one after another, year after year.

Years went past. I flooded and I went down, and each time I came, I found the forest a little bigger. Fallen leaves made a soft, dark floor. Under the leaves lived worms and beetles and white threads of fungus. The roots held the soil, so I could not wash it all away. On the hottest days, it was cooler under the trees than out on the open sand. The leaves breathed water into the air, and the air in the forest stayed damp.

Birds came, and in their droppings came seeds of trees that Jadav had never planted. Deer came, because now there was grass and leaves to eat. And then, one winter, came the elephants. A whole herd waded across my water from the far bank. They walked into the forest as if it had always been there. They ate. They rested in the shade. They left their dung behind, full of more seeds. Later, a rhinoceros came, and even tigers.
For many years, almost nobody outside knew about this forest. Then forest officers, following a herd of elephants, walked into it. They could not believe one man had planted it.

People ask Jadav how he made a forest. They want a secret. I watched the whole thing, so I will tell you what I saw. He did not make the deer, or the birds, or the elephants. He could not have carried a single elephant. What he made was shade, and soil, and damp leaves, and food. He made a place that could give. Everything else walked, flew and crawled in by itself. And each one that came gave something back: the ants made soil, the birds brought seeds, the elephants opened paths.

I still make my sandbars, and I still take them away. That is what I am. But now, when I pass that forest, I slow down a little. The trees drink from me. Their leaves breathe me back into the sky, and the sky rains me onto the hills, and the hills send me down again past the trees. I am no longer sure where the river ends and the forest begins.
story.epiphany: For the parent: the snakes did not die because of the flood. They died because the bare sandbar gave nothing a living thing needs: no shade, no shelter, no food, no damp soil. A habitat is not just a place. It is a place that gives. Jadav could not carry animals to a home. Instead he made the place give shade, soil, water and food, and the animals came by themselves. Each new living thing then changed the place too: ants made soil, birds brought seeds, trees made the air damp. Living things and their habitats make each other. The story also quietly asks what one patient person can do, and who notices.
ask: Why did the snakes on the bare sandbar die?
The old man said, 'Don't carry the animals to a home. Make a home.' What did he mean?
What did the bamboo give that the bare sand did not? Who came because of it?
Jadav carried red ants to the sandbar. How did the ants change the place?
The village laughed at Jadav. Why do you think he kept going?
At the end, the river says it is not sure where the river ends and the forest begins. What do you think it means?

games.title: Who Lives Where?
games.players: 2 to 5 players, or one child playing against the app
games.context: This is a card game about habitats. A habitat is the place where a living thing finds food, water, air, shelter, space and the right warmth. Players put each living thing in the habitat that gives it what it needs, and say why.

printables.title: 24 living-thing cards to cut out
items: Tube worm at a deep sea vent
TWIST: a mudskipper, a fish that walks on mud. Where does it go?
TWIST: a crow. Where can it NOT live?
TWIST: a mangrove tree. Pond or sea?
TWIST: a tiger in the Sundarbans. Forest or sea?

rules: Lay out the six habitat mats. Shuffle the living-thing cards and put them face down. Put the need cards face up in a row.
On your turn, take a card and read it out. Put it on the habitat mat where it lives.
Then pick two need cards. Say how that habitat gives the living thing each of those needs. One leaf token for each good answer.
Anyone can say 'challenge!' if they think the card is on the wrong mat. If the group agrees, the challenger wins a token.
A TWIST card has no single right answer. Say what you think and why. A good reason wins two tokens.
When the cards run out, the player with the most leaf tokens wins.

setup.art: Six paper mats on the floor labelled pond, forest, desert, sea, under a stone and inside a body, with a face-down pile of picture cards.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out the six habitat mats and the cards.

setup.art: A child placing a camel card on the desert mat and holding up two need cards, water and shelter.
setup.caption: 2. Put the card on its habitat. Pick two needs and explain them.

setup.art: A small pile of paper leaf tokens in front of a smiling player.
setup.caption: 3. Win a leaf token for each good reason.

flow.do: 1. Lay the six habitat mats in a circle. 2. Shuffle the 24 living-thing cards and put them face down. 3. Put the six need cards face up in a row.
flow.say: A habitat is a place that gives a living thing what it needs. In this game, we put each living thing where it lives. Then we say how that place gives it two of its needs.
flow.kid: Put the six habitat mats in a circle. Mix up the cards. Put them face down. Put the need cards in a row.
flow.context: This is the first step of Who Lives Where?, a card game about habitats. Here you set up the game.

flow.do: Find the Frog card. Play it together as a practice round.
flow.say: Let's practise with the frog. Where does it go? Now pick two need cards. How does the pond give the frog water? How does it give it food?
flow.kid: Practice card: the frog. Which mat does it go on? Tap your answer.

ask.q: How does a pond give a frog food and shelter?
good: There are insects and worms to eat.
It can hide in the mud or under lotus leaves.

check.q: Where does the frog card go?
options: Desert
Pond
Sea
Inside a body
check.why: A frog's skin must stay wet, and its eggs and tadpoles need fresh water. A pond gives water, insects to eat and mud to hide in. Picking sea usually means thinking all water is the same. But sea water is salty, and most frogs cannot live in it. Picking desert misses that a frog's skin dries out fast in hot, dry air.

flow.do: 1. Take turns. Each player draws a card, reads it and places it. 2. They pick two need cards and explain them. 3. Give a leaf token for each good reason.
flow.say: When you place your card, tell me two ways that habitat looks after it. If you think someone's card is on the wrong mat, say challenge.
flow.kid: Take turns. Read your card. Put it on a mat. Pick two needs. Say how the habitat gives them.
flow.parent: Good reasons are specific. 'The forest gives the hornbill fruit to eat and tall trees to nest in' is better than 'it lives there'. Tricky cards: the woodlouse goes under a stone, because it needs damp and dark. The tube worm goes in the sea, at the deep vents. Bacteria in your tummy go on 'inside a body': the body gives them food, water and warmth.

flow.do: When a TWIST card comes up, everyone says where they would put it and why. Do not look for one right answer.
flow.say: This card is a twist. There may be more than one good answer. Where would you put it? Why?
flow.kid: A TWIST card! There may be two right answers. Where would you put it? Say why.

ask.q: Where does a mangrove tree go: pond or sea?
good: Both, sort of. It grows where the river meets the sea, in water that is part salty.
It is on the edge between two habitats.

flow.think: If some living things live on the edge between two habitats, are habitats really separate?

flow.do: 1. Count the leaf tokens to find the winner. 2. Look at which mat has the most cards.
flow.say: Look at the mats. Which habitat got the most living things? Which got the fewest? Is that what you expected?
flow.kid: Count your leaf tokens. Who won? Which mat has the most cards? Why do you think so?
flow.think: We put bacteria on the 'inside a body' mat. Are you a habitat too?

games.title: Nature Bingo: Habitat Hunt
games.players: 1 to 4 players, with a grown-up outdoors
games.context: This is an outdoor bingo game. You walk in a park, a garden or around your building, and look for small habitats and the living things that use them.

printables.title: A bingo sheet of 16 squares (4 by 4)
items: a living thing under a stone
something living in a crack in a wall
a hole that something lives in
a leaf that has been nibbled
an animal drinking or a place it could drink
a living thing on another living thing (like moss on a tree)
a flower being visited by an insect
a place with no living thing you can see

printables.title: Find log
items: What it gives the living thing (food, water, shelter, space, warmth)

rules: Each player gets a bingo sheet and a pencil.
Walk slowly together with a grown-up. When you find something on your sheet, show the others and tick it.
For each tick, say what that place gives to the living thing there.
Four ticks in a row, across, down or corner to corner, is BINGO.
Keep playing until everyone has a bingo, or for 20 minutes. Then share your best find.

setup.art: A 4 by 4 bingo sheet with small pictures in each square: a stone, a crack, a web, a hole, a nibbled leaf.
setup.caption: 1. Each player takes a bingo sheet and a pencil.

setup.art: Two children and a grown-up crouched by a wall, pointing at moss growing in a crack.
setup.caption: 2. Walk slowly. Look high, low and in small places.

setup.art: A bingo sheet with four ticks in a row and a child cheering.
setup.caption: 3. Tick what you find. Four in a row is bingo.

flow.do: 1. Print a bingo sheet for each player. 2. Choose a safe place to walk: a park, a garden or around your building. 3. Agree on the rule: we look and lift gently, and put everything back.
flow.say: Today we're habitat hunters. We are looking for small habitats and who lives in them. If we lift a stone, we put it back gently, the same way up.
flow.kid: You are a habitat hunter today. Look for small homes. If you lift a stone, put it back gently.
flow.parent: Stay with your child outdoors. Do not put hands into holes or deep cracks, where scorpions or snakes may hide. Lift stones towards you, so anything underneath runs away from you.
flow.context: This is the first step of Nature Bingo, an outdoor game. You hunt for small habitats and the living things using them.

flow.do: Walk slowly. Help your child spot things on the sheet. For each tick, ask what that place gives.
flow.say: You found a web in the corner of the gate. What does that corner give the spider? Food, because insects fly past. Shelter, because it is out of the rain.
flow.kid: Walk slowly. Look up, down and into small places. For each find, say what the place gives.

check.q: You lift a flat stone and find woodlice underneath. What does the space under the stone give them?
options: Bright sunlight
Damp and shade
Salty water
Nothing, they are just lost
check.why: Under a stone it is darker, cooler and damper than the open ground. Woodlice dry out fast, so they need damp, shady places. Picking bright sunlight is the opposite: in the sun, woodlice dry out. Picking 'lost' misses that many animals choose a place because of what it gives them.

flow.do: 1. Count ticks and find the bingos. 2. Each player shares their best find.
flow.say: Which was your favourite find? What did that place give the living thing?
flow.kid: Did you get bingo? Show your best find. What did that place give?
flow.think: Did you find a square with no living thing you could see? Do you think it was really empty?

flow.do: Go back to the square 'a place with no living thing you can see'. Look again at it with a magnifying glass, if you have one.
flow.say: Let's look again at the place that seemed empty. With a magnifying glass, can we find anything now? Remember, microbes are too small to see even with this.
flow.kid: Look again at the 'empty' place. Use a magnifying glass. Is it really empty?
flow.parent: Many 'empty' places turn out to have tiny mites, springtails or moss. Even a bare stone usually has invisible microbes on it. This is a good moment to say: empty-looking is not the same as empty.

experiments.title: Damp or Dry? The Woodlouse Choice Tray
experiments.question: Do woodlice choose damp places or dry places?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. If ten woodlice can walk anywhere in a tray, will more of them end up on the damp side, the dry side, or will they spread out evenly?
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, change only one thing: damp or dry. Keep both sides equally dark, by covering the whole tray. Count every 5 minutes. Then do it again with the damp side swapped, because the woodlice might just like one end of the tray.

materials.item: a shallow tray or a big steel plate with a rim
2 sheets of kitchen paper or tissue
a little water
a sheet of cardboard or a newspaper to cover the tray
8 to 10 woodlice from under a flowerpot or a stone
a soft paintbrush or a spoon, to move them gently
a timer and the results table

experiments.safety: Wash hands after handling soil and animals. Move woodlice with a soft brush or a spoon, not your fingers. Keep them out of the sun. Put them back where you found them within 30 minutes.

schedule.what: Collect woodlice. Set up the damp and dry tray. Count every 5 minutes for 15 minutes. Swap sides and test again. Put the woodlice back.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw two bars, one for the damp side and one for the dry side, at 15 minutes. Write one sentence for what you think, one for what you saw and one for why.
experiments.context: This is the choice tray experiment. You give some woodlice a tray with a damp side and a dry side, and count where they go. A woodlouse is a small grey creature with 14 legs that lives under stones and flowerpots.

setup.art: A shallow tray with a damp, darker kitchen paper on the left half and a dry, white paper on the right half.
setup.caption: 1. Make one half of the tray damp and one half dry.

setup.art: A child gently tipping ten grey woodlice from a spoon onto the line in the middle of the tray.
setup.caption: 2. Put the woodlice gently in the middle.

setup.art: The tray covered with cardboard and a phone timer showing 5 minutes beside it.
setup.caption: 3. Cover the whole tray. Wait 5 minutes.

setup.art: The cover lifted and a child counting woodlice, with most of them on the damp side.
setup.caption: 4. Lift the cover. Count each side. Do this three times.

flow.do: 1. Go to a garden, a park or a balcony with plants. 2. Lift a flowerpot or a flat stone. 3. Gently brush 8 to 10 woodlice into a cup with a little damp soil. 4. Put the stone back.
flow.say: Let's look under this pot. These small grey creatures are woodlice. They are cousins of crabs and prawns, not insects. We will borrow them for a short test and bring them back.
flow.kid: Lift a flowerpot gently. Find the small grey woodlice. Brush 10 of them into a cup. Put the pot back.
flow.parent: If you cannot find woodlice, try under fallen leaves or a damp brick. After rain, earthworms work for this test too. Lift stones towards you in case anything is underneath. Do not put fingers under stones.
flow.context: This is the first step of the choice tray experiment. You find woodlice to test whether they choose damp or dry places.

flow.do: 1. Put one sheet of kitchen paper on each half of the tray. 2. Sprinkle water on the left sheet until it is damp but not dripping. 3. Leave the right sheet dry.
flow.say: We change only one thing: one side is damp and the other is dry. Everything else is the same. That makes it a fair test.
flow.kid: Put paper on both halves of the tray. Make the left side damp. Keep the right side dry.

ask.q: Before we start, where do you think the woodlice will go?
good: The damp side, because they live under damp stones.

flow.do: 1. Tip the woodlice gently onto the middle of the tray. 2. Cover the whole tray with cardboard so both sides are dark. 3. After 5 minutes, lift the cover and count woodlice on each side. 4. Cover again and count at 10 and 15 minutes. 5. Write the numbers in the table.
flow.say: Why do we cover the whole tray? So both sides are equally dark. Then only dampness is different. Let's count quietly and quickly, then cover them again.
flow.kid: Put the woodlice in the middle. Cover the tray. Every 5 minutes, lift and count each side. Write the numbers down.
flow.parent: Woodlice usually gather on the damp side within 10 minutes. They also slow down and bunch together there. A few may stay on the dry side or wander. That is normal. Now swap the damp paper to the other side and test once more, so you know they are choosing damp and not one end of the tray.

chart.title: Made-up example: how to fill in the table

flow.do: Look at the 15-minute numbers together and compare them with the guess.
flow.say: Look at the numbers at 15 minutes. Where did most woodlice go? Was your guess right?
flow.kid: Look at your numbers at 15 minutes. Where did most go? Were you right?

check.q: In the choice tray, 8 woodlice went to the damp side and 2 to the dry side. What does this suggest?
options: Woodlice choose damp places
Woodlice choose dry places
Woodlice go anywhere by chance
Woodlice like the left side of a tray
check.why: Most woodlice ended on the damp side, so they seem to choose damp places. That fits where we find them, under damp stones and pots. Picking 'by chance' would fit if they had spread out evenly, about 5 and 5. Picking 'the left side' is a good worry. That is why scientists swap the damp side and test again.

chart.title: Made-up example: woodlice on each side after 15 minutes
chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be different.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Let's finish like real scientists. Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Finish like a scientist. Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: woodlice choose damp places. What I saw: after 15 minutes, 8 were on the damp side and 2 on the dry side, and it was the same when we swapped. Why: woodlice dry out easily, so a damp place is part of their habitat.

flow.do: Put the woodlice back under the same stone or pot, with a little damp soil. Wash your hands.
flow.say: Thank you, woodlice. Let's put them back home. Their habitat is under that pot, not in our tray.
flow.kid: Take the woodlice back to their pot. Put them down gently. Wash your hands.
flow.think: The woodlice found the damp side without eyes that see much. How do you think they knew?

example_chart.title: Made-up example: woodlice on each side after 15 minutes
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be different.

experiments.title: One Garden, Five Different Worlds
experiments.question: Is it the same temperature and dampness everywhere in one garden, or do small places have their own weather?
experiments.predict: Before you measure, guess. Put these five places in order from hottest to coolest: an open sunny path, a patch of grass, under a bush, under a stone and under a pile of fallen leaves.
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, measure all five places at about the same time of day, with the same thermometer. Leave the thermometer in each place for the same time, 2 minutes. Feel each place for dampness with the back of the same hand.
results_table: Damp or dry (1 = dry, 5 = very damp)

materials.item: a thermometer, a digital one is easiest
a timer
a magnifying glass
a pencil and the results table

experiments.safety: Do this with a grown-up. Lift stones towards you, so anything underneath runs away from you. Do not touch centipedes or scorpions. On a very hot day, wear a cap.

schedule.what: Measure temperature and dampness in five small places in one garden, at midday. Count living things in each. Draw a bar chart.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw a bar for each place, as tall as its temperature. Next to each bar, write how many living things you found there.
experiments.context: This is the five worlds experiment. You measure how hot and how damp five small places in one garden are, and count who lives in each. A thermometer measures how hot something is, in degrees Celsius.

setup.art: A digital thermometer lying on an open sunny path, with a phone timer showing 2 minutes.
setup.caption: 1. Put the thermometer on the sunny path for 2 minutes. Read it.

setup.art: A hand lifting a flat stone, and the thermometer tip pushed into the damp soil underneath.
setup.caption: 2. Measure under a stone, under a bush, in grass and under leaves.

setup.art: A child with a magnifying glass counting small animals in a pile of leaves, with a tally on a notebook.
setup.caption: 3. Count the living things in each place.

flow.do: 1. Choose a garden, a park corner or a big pot with plants. 2. Find five places: an open sunny path, grass, under a bush, under a stone and under fallen leaves. 3. Ask your child to put them in order, hottest first.
flow.say: Is it the same everywhere in this garden? Let's guess which of these five places is the hottest, and which is the coolest.
flow.kid: Find five places: a sunny path, grass, under a bush, under a stone, under leaves. Which is hottest? Guess first.
flow.context: This is the first step of the five worlds experiment. You choose five small places in one garden and guess which is hottest.

flow.do: 1. Put the thermometer in the first place for 2 minutes, then read it. 2. Touch the ground there with the back of your hand and give it a dampness score from 1 to 5. 3. Count any living things you can see, using the magnifying glass. 4. Write it all in the table. 5. Do the same in all five places.
flow.say: We leave the thermometer for 2 minutes in each place, so every place gets the same time. That keeps it fair. Now feel the ground. Is it dry, or damp?
flow.kid: Put the thermometer in each place for 2 minutes. Read it. Feel the ground. Count the living things. Write it all down.
flow.parent: On a sunny day you will often see 10 degrees or more difference between the open path and under the stone or the leaves. The cooler, damper places usually have more living things.

chart.title: Made-up example: how to fill in the table

flow.do: Help your child draw a bar chart: one bar for each place, as tall as its temperature.
flow.say: Let's turn the numbers into a picture. Each place gets a bar. The taller the bar, the hotter the place.
flow.kid: Draw one bar for each place. Make it as tall as the temperature. Write how many living things you found next to it.

check.q: In the five worlds experiment, the sunny path was 41 degrees and under the leaves was 28 degrees. Which place had more living things, and why?
options: The sunny path, because animals like heat
Under the leaves, because it is cooler and damper
Both the same, because it is one garden
Neither, because animals only live in forests
check.why: Under the leaves it is cooler and damper, and there is food from rotting leaves. Most small animals dry out in hot sun, so they live there. Picking 'both the same' misses the point of the test: one garden holds many microhabitats with different weather. Picking 'only forests' forgets the woodlice and ants we just counted.

chart.title: Made-up example: temperature in five places in one garden at midday
chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be different.

flow.do: Compare the results with the guess. Then ask your child to say or write: what I think, what I saw, and why.
flow.say: Were your guesses right? Now finish like a scientist. What do you think? What did you see? Why?
flow.kid: Were you right? Say three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: small places in one garden have very different weather. What I saw: the sunny path was 41 degrees, and under the leaves was 28 degrees, with 14 living things. Why: shade and leaves keep the sun off and hold water in.
flow.think: If one garden has five different worlds, how many worlds might there be in a whole forest?

flow.do: Put back every stone and leaf pile the way you found it.
flow.say: Let's put everything back. Each of these places is somebody's home.
flow.kid: Put back every stone and leaf the way you found it. These are homes.

example_chart.title: Made-up example: temperature in five places in one garden at midday
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be different.

experiments.title: Does a Tree Give Water to the Air?
experiments.question: Do leaves give off water into the air? Is that one way a forest keeps itself damp?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. If you tie a clear plastic bag around a leafy branch in the sun, what will you see inside the bag after one hour?
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, tie a second bag around a branch with all its leaves taken off, or around a dry stick, in the same sunny place. Both bags stay on for the same time. Then only the leaves are different.
results_table: What I saw inside after 1 hour

materials.item: 2 clear plastic bags, clean and dry
2 pieces of string or rubber bands
a leafy branch of a bush or small tree in the sun, and a bare dry stick
a teaspoon or a dropper

experiments.safety: Choose a plant that is not thorny or poisonous, such as a hibiscus, guava or tulsi plant. Take the bag off after the test, so the leaves can breathe.

schedule.what: Tie a bag around a leafy branch and one around a bare stick. Wait one hour. Collect and compare the water.

experiments.record: Draw both bags after one hour. Write how much water collected in each.
experiments.context: This is the tree water experiment. You tie a clear plastic bag around a leafy branch in the sun, and see whether the leaves give off water into the air.

setup.art: A clear plastic bag being slipped over a leafy hibiscus branch in sunshine.
setup.caption: 1. Slip a clear bag over a leafy branch in the sun.

setup.art: The bag tied at the stem with string, and a second bag tied over a bare dry stick next to it.
setup.caption: 2. Tie it tight. Tie a second bag over a bare stick.

setup.art: After an hour, the bag on the leafy branch misty with drops collecting at the bottom; the bag on the stick still clear.
setup.caption: 3. After one hour, look and collect the drops.

flow.do: 1. Find a leafy branch in the sun. 2. Slip a clear plastic bag over the end, with plenty of leaves inside. 3. Tie the bag tightly around the stem. 4. Tie a second bag over a bare stick in the same sunny place.
flow.say: We'll trap the air around these leaves. The second bag, over a bare stick, is our comparison. Only the leaves are different.
flow.kid: Put a clear bag over a leafy branch in the sun. Tie it tight. Put another bag over a bare stick.
flow.context: This is the first step of the tree water experiment. You trap the air around some leaves in a clear bag.

flow.do: Leave both bags in the sun for one hour. Set a timer.
flow.say: Now we wait an hour. What do you think will happen in each bag?
flow.kid: Wait one hour. What will happen inside each bag? Guess.
flow.wait: Leave the bags for one hour, then come back.

flow.do: 1. Look at both bags. 2. Gently shake the drops in the leafy bag down to one corner. 3. Untie it and pour the water into a spoon. 4. Do the same with the other bag. 5. Write what you found.
flow.say: Look, the leafy bag is misty and has drops in it. Where did that water come from? We didn't pour any in.
flow.kid: Look at both bags. Which one has water inside? Collect the drops in a spoon.
flow.parent: On a sunny day the leafy bag is usually misty within 15 minutes. After an hour there may be a teaspoon of water or more. The bare-stick bag stays almost dry. This shows the water came out of the leaves. Plants pull water up from their roots and let it out through tiny holes in their leaves.

check.q: In the tree water experiment, the bag on the leafy branch got misty with drops of water. Where did the water come from?
options: From the leaves, which give off water into the air
From the rain
From the plastic bag
From the string
check.why: The bag was dry and closed, so the water came out of the leaves. Plants pull water up from the soil through their roots and let it out from tiny holes in their leaves. Picking 'from the rain' misses that the bag was closed and it did not rain. The bare-stick bag, which stayed dry, shows the plastic was not the cause.

flow.do: Talk about what this means for a whole forest. Then ask for what I think, what I saw and why.
flow.say: One branch gave a spoonful in an hour. A big tree has thousands of branches. A forest has millions of trees. All that water goes up into the air. That is one reason a forest stays damp, and it helps make clouds and rain. Now tell me: what do you think, what did you see, and why?
flow.kid: One branch gave a spoonful. Think of a whole forest! Now say three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer: What I think: leaves give off water into the air. What I saw: the leafy bag had drops after an hour, the stick bag stayed dry. Why: plants pull water from the soil and let it out through their leaves. This is why a forest makes its habitat damp, and why cutting a forest can make a place drier.
flow.think: If a forest helps make its own rain, what might happen to the rain if the forest is cut down?

flow.do: Take both bags off the plant.
flow.say: Let's take the bag off, so the leaves can breathe again.
flow.kid: Take the bags off the plant. Let the leaves breathe.

activities.title: Under the Stone

materials.item: a flat stone, a brick or a flowerpot that has been lying on soil for a while
a magnifying glass, if you have one

activities.safety: A grown-up lifts the stone, tilting it towards themselves, so anything underneath runs away from them. Do not touch centipedes or scorpions. Put the stone back gently.

schedule.what: Guess, lift a stone, count who lives under it, and notice how it feels.

activities.record: Draw what you saw under the stone. Write your guess and the real number of living things.
activities.context: This is a short noticing activity to start the unit. You lift a stone and look at the small world hiding under it.

setup.art: A child and a grown-up crouching by a flat stone on garden soil, the child holding up fingers to guess.
setup.caption: 1. Guess how many living things are under the stone.

setup.art: A grown-up's hand tilting a stone towards themselves, revealing woodlice, an earthworm, ants and pale roots on dark damp soil.
setup.caption: 2. A grown-up lifts it gently. Look quickly.

setup.art: The child touching the damp soil under the stone and then the dry soil next to it with the back of her hand.
setup.caption: 3. Feel the soil under the stone and next to it.

flow.do: 1. Find a stone, a brick or a pot that has been lying on soil for some days. 2. Ask your child to guess how many living things are under it.
flow.say: Before we lift it, guess. How many living things do you think are hiding under this stone?
flow.kid: Look at the stone. Do not lift it yet. How many living things are under it? Guess.
flow.context: This is the first step of Under the Stone. You guess how many living things hide under a stone.

flow.do: 1. Lift the stone towards yourself. 2. Look quickly, because many animals will run. 3. Count everything you see: woodlice, ants, worms, beetles, centipedes, roots, white fungus threads.
flow.say: Quick, look! What do you notice? Let's count everything that is alive. What do you wonder about?
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to lift the stone. Look fast! Count every living thing. What do you notice?

ask.q: What do you notice? What do you wonder?
good: It's dark and wet under there.
Why are they all hiding here?
Where do they go when it rains?

flow.do: 1. Touch the soil under the stone with the back of your hand. 2. Touch the open soil next to it. 3. Put the stone back gently, the same way up.
flow.say: Feel the soil under the stone. Now feel the soil next to it. Which is cooler? Which is damper? Why do you think so many animals live under here, and not out there?
flow.kid: Feel under the stone. Then feel the soil next to it. Which is cooler and damper? Put the stone back gently.

check.q: Why do woodlice and worms live under a stone and not on the open ground next to it?
options: Under the stone is cooler, darker and damper
The stone is food for them
They are trapped and cannot get out
The open ground is too wet
check.why: Under a stone it is cooler, darker and damper. Woodlice and worms dry out quickly, so this small place gives them what they need. A place like this is called a microhabitat. Picking 'trapped' misses that they ran away when the stone was lifted, then crawled back under it. Picking 'too wet' is the opposite of what your hand felt.

flow.think: Is the space under the stone a whole world? Whose habitat is it?

activities.title: What Does the Crow Need?

materials.item: a notebook and a pencil

activities.safety: Watch animals from a distance. Do not go near street dogs or monkeys. Stay with a grown-up outdoors.

schedule.what: Choose one animal near home. Find where it gets each of its needs.

activities.record: Draw your animal in the middle of a page. Draw six arrows to where it gets food, water, air, shelter, space and warmth.
activities.context: In this activity, you choose one animal near your home, like a crow, a pigeon, a squirrel or a gecko. Then you find where it gets each thing it needs. Together, those places are its habitat.

setup.art: A child at a balcony pointing at a crow on a wire, with a notebook open.
setup.caption: 1. Choose one animal you can see near home.

setup.art: A child drawing arrows from a crow in the middle of a page to a dustbin, a water tank, a tree and the sky.
setup.caption: 2. Find where it gets each of its six needs.

setup.art: A finished page with a crow in the middle and six labelled arrows: food, water, air, shelter, space, warmth.
setup.caption: 3. Draw your animal and its six needs.

flow.do: Go to a window, a balcony or the gate. Choose one animal you can see often, such as a crow, a pigeon, a squirrel or a gecko.
flow.say: Let's choose one animal we see every day. We will be detectives and find out what its habitat gives it.
flow.kid: Choose one animal you see every day. A crow? A squirrel? A gecko on the wall?
flow.context: This is the first step of What Does the Crow Need? You choose an animal near your home to study.

flow.do: 1. Watch your animal for a few minutes. 2. For each of the six needs, ask: where does it get this? 3. Write or draw each answer.
flow.say: Where does the crow find food? Water? Where does it sleep or nest? Where is it safe? Is there enough space for it? Where does it go when it is very hot?
flow.kid: Watch your animal. Where does it get food? Water? Shelter? Space? Where does it go when it's hot?
flow.parent: Good answers are places you can point to: 'the crow drinks from the leaking tap', 'it nests in the neem tree', 'it rests in shade on the water tank at noon'. If your child does not know, it is fine to say 'we don't know yet' and watch again tomorrow.

flow.do: Draw the animal in the middle of a page, with six arrows to the places you found.
flow.say: Let's draw it. All these places together are your animal's habitat. Its habitat isn't one spot. It is everywhere it gets what it needs.
flow.kid: Draw your animal in the middle. Draw six arrows to where it gets each need. That is its habitat!

check.q: A crow drinks from a tap, eats from a dustbin, nests in a neem tree and flies over the whole street. What is its habitat?
options: Only the neem tree
Only the dustbin
All of these places together
The sky
check.why: A habitat is every place where a living thing gets what it needs. For this crow, that is the tap, the dustbin, the tree and the street together. Picking 'only the neem tree' mixes up a habitat with a home or nest. The nest is just the shelter part of the habitat.

flow.think: If the neem tree were cut down, what would the crow have to do?

activities.title: Square Metre Safari

materials.item: 4 metres of string or wool
4 sticks or pencils to push into the ground
a measuring tape or a 1 metre ruler
a magnifying glass
a notebook and a pencil

activities.safety: Do this with a grown-up. Do not put hands into holes. Wash your hands afterwards.

schedule.what: Mark out two squares, one in a lawn or open patch and one under a tree. Count the kinds of living things in each.

activities.record: Make a tally for each square: how many different kinds of living things you found. Then draw two bars.
activities.context: This activity is how real scientists study habitats. You mark out a square, 1 metre on each side, and count every kind of living thing inside it. Then you compare two squares.

setup.art: Four sticks pushed into grass in a square, with string tied around them, and a measuring tape along one side showing 1 metre.
setup.caption: 1. Mark out a square, 1 metre on each side, with sticks and string.

setup.art: A child lying on her tummy at the edge of the square, looking through a magnifying glass at grass, ants and a tiny flower.
setup.caption: 2. Look closely. Count every different kind of living thing.

setup.art: A second string square marked out under a tree, on fallen leaves.
setup.caption: 3. Mark a second square in a different place. Count again.

flow.do: 1. Push 4 sticks into the ground to make a square, 1 metre on each side. 2. Tie string around the sticks. 3. Do this in an open lawn or patch of grass.
flow.say: Scientists who study habitats often use a square like this. It is called a quadrat. We will count every different kind of living thing inside it.
flow.kid: Make a square with 4 sticks and string. Each side is 1 metre. Scientists call this a quadrat.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Square Metre Safari. You mark out a square of ground to count the living things in it.

flow.do: 1. Look slowly at every part of the square, using the magnifying glass. 2. Count the different kinds of plants and animals, not how many of each. 3. Make a tally mark for each new kind.
flow.say: We're counting kinds, not numbers. Ten ants of the same kind count as one kind. A different ant counts as a new kind. Look at the soil, the grass and the tiny flowers.
flow.kid: Look closely at every part of the square. Make a tally for each new kind you find.
