flow.parent: Children often find 5 to 15 kinds in a lawn: grasses, small weeds, ants, a spider, a beetle, a worm. Under a tree, with fallen leaves, there are usually more. You do not need names. 'Tiny brown jumping bug' is a fine name.

flow.do: Move the string square to a different place, such as under a tree, by a wall or near a tap. Count the kinds again.
flow.say: Now let's try a different place. Where do you think we will find more kinds of living things?
flow.kid: Move your square under a tree, or near a tap. Count the kinds again. Which has more?

check.q: In the Square Metre Safari, a lawn square had 6 kinds of living things. A square under a tree with fallen leaves had 14 kinds. Why might the tree square have more?
options: It gives more shade, damp, shelter and food from leaves
Trees scare animals away from lawns
We counted it later in the day
Squares under trees are bigger
check.why: Under a tree there is shade, damp soil, shelter under leaves and food from rotting leaves. More needs are met, for more kinds of living things. Picking 'counted later in the day' is a sensible worry. A fair test would count both squares at about the same time. Picking 'bigger' forgets that both squares were 1 metre on each side.

flow.do: Compare the two tallies. Draw two bars.
flow.say: Which square had more kinds? What did that place give that the other did not?
flow.kid: Draw a bar for each square. Which had more kinds? Why do you think so?
flow.think: Scientists call the number of different kinds of living things biodiversity. Which places near your home do you think have the most?

activities.title: Nature Map of Our Walk

materials.item: a big sheet of paper
crayons or colour pencils
a small bag or box for fallen things

activities.safety: Collect only fallen things: leaves, feathers, seeds, twigs. Do not pick flowers or take anything alive. Wash your hands after the walk.

schedule.what: Walk, collect fallen things, note where each was found, and draw a nature map.

activities.record: Draw a map of your walk. Mark where each thing was found, and colour the map by habitat: shady, sunny, wet, dry.
activities.context: This activity comes from a DeepKids nature walk idea. You walk in a park or around your area, collect fallen things, and draw a map of where each one came from.

setup.art: A child picking up a fallen feather near a tree, a small cloth bag in her other hand.
setup.caption: 1. Walk and collect fallen things. Remember where each one was.

setup.art: A big sheet of paper with a hand-drawn path, a tree, a tap and a grass patch, and small things glued next to each.
setup.caption: 2. Draw a map of your walk. Put each thing where you found it.

setup.art: The same map coloured in green for shade, yellow for sun and blue for wet places.
setup.caption: 3. Colour each part: shady, sunny or wet.

flow.do: 1. Walk slowly in a park or around your building. 2. Pick up fallen things: leaves, feathers, seeds, snail shells. 3. For each, say out loud where you found it: at the tree base, in the grass, near water.
flow.say: Let's collect only fallen things. Each time we pick something up, let's say where we found it. Was it shady or sunny there? Wet or dry?
flow.kid: Walk slowly. Pick up only fallen things. Say where you found each one. Shady or sunny? Wet or dry?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Nature Map. You go on a walk and collect fallen things, remembering where each one came from.

flow.do: At home, draw the path of the walk on a big sheet. Mark the trees, the grass, any water. Put each thing on the map where it was found.
flow.say: Let's draw our walk. Here's the gate, here's the big tree, here's the tap. Where did the feather go? Where did the snail shell go?
flow.kid: Draw your walk. Put each thing where you found it.
flow.parent: Patterns often show up: snail shells and moss near water and shade, dry seeds and feathers in sunny open places. Point these out only if your child does not notice them first.

flow.do: Colour the map: green for shady places, yellow for sunny, blue for wet. Look for patterns.
flow.say: Look at the colours. Did different things come from shady places and sunny places? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Colour the shady parts green, sunny parts yellow, wet parts blue. What pattern do you see?

check.q: On a nature map, snail shells were found only near a leaking tap and in shady places. What does this suggest about snails?
options: Snails need damp, shady places
Snails like sunny paths
Snails are found everywhere equally
Snails live only in the sea
check.why: Snails dry out easily, so they live where it is damp and shady. The map shows that pattern. Picking 'everywhere equally' does not fit the map, which shows them in only some places. Some snails do live in the sea, but these were garden snails, found near a tap.

activities.title: Four Homes: Act and Move

materials.item: open space to move
4 sheets of paper with POND, FOREST, DESERT and SEA written on them

activities.safety: Clear the space of sharp corners and things that could break.

schedule.what: Move like the four habitats, then act out a meeting of the four habitats.

activities.record: Draw yourself as your favourite habitat, and write one thing it gives and one thing that is hard there.
activities.context: This is a movement and drama activity from DeepKids' ideas. You move like each of the four habitats, then act out a meeting where they talk about what they give.

setup.art: Four paper signs on the floor in four corners of a room: pond, forest, desert and sea.
setup.caption: 1. Put the four habitat signs in four corners.

setup.art: A child swaying with arms up like tall forest trees; another child lying very still like a desert at noon.
setup.caption: 2. Move like each habitat when a grown-up calls its name.

setup.art: Four children sitting in a circle wearing paper signs saying pond, forest, desert and sea, talking.
setup.caption: 3. Act out a meeting of the four habitats.

flow.do: 1. Put the four signs in four corners. 2. Call out a habitat. Your child runs to that corner and moves like it: the pond ripples, the forest sways, the desert lies still at noon then comes alive at night, the sea rolls in waves. 3. Call out a living thing too, like 'a frog in the pond', and your child moves like it.
flow.say: When I say a habitat, run to its corner and become it. Desert! Now it's noon, lie very still and hot. Now it's night. Who comes out? Sea! Roll like waves. Now dive down to the dark bottom.
flow.kid: When a grown-up calls a habitat, run to that corner. Become it! Desert at noon: lie still. Desert at night: come alive!
flow.context: This is the first step of Four Homes: Act and Move. You move like each of the four habitats.

flow.do: Act out a meeting of the four habitats. Each player is one habitat. Each one says what it gives easily, and what is hard there. Then they argue: who is the best home?
flow.say: I am the desert. I give lots of sunshine and space. But I have very little water. Who are you? What do you give? And who would want to live in you?
flow.kid: Be one habitat. Say what you give. Say what is hard in you. Who is the best home?
flow.parent: Let the argument go on. A good ending is when the children see there is no single best home: each one is best for some living things. If your child is alone, take turns playing two habitats each.

check.q: In the habitat meeting, which habitat is the best home?
options: The forest, because it has the most food
The sea, because it is the biggest
There is no single best one. Each habitat is best for the living things that fit it.
The pond, because it is the smallest
check.why: Each habitat gives some things easily and makes others hard. A camel does best in the desert, a fish in water. Picking forest or sea is a fine opinion, but think of the camel. The forest would be a poor home for it, and the sea would kill it.

flow.do: Lie down quietly for one minute. Imagine you are the deep sea floor: dark, cold and still. Then imagine the hot vent and its crowd of worms.
flow.say: Close your eyes. You are the deep sea floor. Dark. Cold. Still. Now, a crack opens and hot water pours out. Feel the crowd of life arrive.
flow.kid: Lie still. Close your eyes. You are the dark sea floor. Now hot water bubbles up. Life arrives!
flow.think: Which habitat did you feel most at home in? Why?

activities.title: Curd Town: A Habitat in a Bowl

materials.item: 2 small steel bowls
1 cup of warm milk (boiled, then cooled until it feels just warm on your wrist)
1 teaspoon of curd from the last batch or from a shop
space in the fridge

activities.safety: A grown-up boils the milk and cools it. Use only clean bowls and spoons. Eat only the curd that set in the warm place, and only if it smells fresh.

schedule.what: Mix curd into warm milk in two bowls. Put one in a warm place and one in the fridge.
Compare the two bowls. Which became curd? Why?

activities.record: Draw both bowls on day 2. Write which one set, and which habitat suited the bacteria.
activities.context: This activity shows that tiny living things called bacteria have habitats too. You set curd in two bowls: one warm and one cold. Curd is made by bacteria growing in milk.

setup.art: A grown-up pouring warm milk into two steel bowls, and a child adding a spoon of curd to each.
setup.caption: 1. Add a spoon of curd to warm milk in two bowls.

setup.art: One bowl covered with a plate in a warm kitchen corner; the other on a fridge shelf.
setup.caption: 2. Put one bowl somewhere warm and one in the fridge.

setup.art: Next morning: the warm bowl holding firm white curd on a tilted spoon; the fridge bowl still runny milk.
setup.caption: 3. Next day, compare. Which became curd?

flow.do: 1. A grown-up boils milk and lets it cool until it feels just warm on the wrist. 2. Pour half into each bowl. 3. Stir one teaspoon of curd into each. 4. Cover both. Put one in a warm place in the kitchen and one in the fridge.
flow.say: Curd is made by bacteria, tiny living things. The spoon of curd adds lots of them to the milk. Milk gives them food and water. Let's see which place is the right habitat for them: warm or cold.
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to warm the milk. Add a spoon of curd to each bowl. Put one somewhere warm. Put one in the fridge.
flow.context: This is the first step of Curd Town. You add bacteria from curd to warm milk, and keep one bowl warm and one cold.

flow.do: Leave both bowls overnight.
flow.say: Now we wait until tomorrow. The bacteria will be busy, if their habitat suits them.
flow.kid: Wait until tomorrow morning. Which bowl will turn into curd?
flow.wait: Leave both bowls overnight, about 8 hours.

flow.do: Next day, tilt both bowls gently. Compare them.
flow.say: Look. The warm bowl has set into curd. The cold one is still milk. Why? The bacteria had food and water in both bowls. But only one gave them the right warmth.
flow.kid: Tilt both bowls. Which one is curd? Which is still milk? Why?

check.q: In Curd Town, the warm bowl turned into curd and the fridge bowl stayed as milk. Why?
options: Warmth is part of the bacteria's habitat. They grow well when warm and very slowly when cold.
The fridge killed all the milk
The fridge bowl had no bacteria
Curd only forms in steel bowls
check.why: Both bowls had bacteria, food and water. Only the warm one had the right warmth, so the bacteria grew and turned the milk into curd. In the cold, they barely grow. Picking 'no bacteria' forgets that we added curd to both. This is why curd sets slowly in winter.

flow.think: Your tummy is warm, wet and full of food. What does that make it for bacteria?

projects.title: Make a Habitat Corner: Water and Shelter for Wild Visitors

materials.item: a shallow clay bowl or a wide plate
a few stones to put in the bowl
an empty tin or a plastic bottle cut open, with no sharp edges
dry twigs, hollow stems, straw, dry leaves and pine cones
string
a notebook for the visitor diary

projects.safety: A grown-up cuts the tin or bottle and covers any sharp edges with tape. Keep the bowl shallow, with stones in it, so small birds and insects cannot drown. Change the water every day, so mosquitoes cannot breed in it.

schedule.what: Choose a spot. Set up the water bowl. Build a small bug shelter. Start the visitor diary.
Change the water. Watch for 5 minutes. Write any visitors.
Change the water. Watch for 5 minutes. Write any visitors.
Watch for 10 minutes. Check the bug shelter gently. Count the week's visitors.
Change the water. Watch for 5 minutes.
Count all the visitors. Make a pictograph. Decide what to add or change.

projects.record: Keep a visitor diary: the date, the time, who came, and what they did (drank, bathed, rested, hid). On the last day, make a pictograph of all the visitors.
projects.context: This is a two-week project. You make a small habitat corner on a balcony, a window ledge or in a garden, with water and shelter, and keep a diary of the wild visitors who use it.

setup.art: A shallow clay bowl with three stones in it, full of water, on a balcony ledge in partial shade.
setup.caption: 1. Put a shallow bowl of water with stones in it in a shady spot.

setup.art: A cut tin packed tightly with hollow stems and twigs, tied with string to a railing.
setup.caption: 2. Make a bug shelter: a tin packed with hollow stems and twigs.

setup.art: A child's notebook page with a table of dates, times and little drawings of a bulbul, a bee and a butterfly.
setup.caption: 3. Watch every few days and write down the visitors.

flow.do: 1. Choose a spot: a balcony, a window ledge or a corner of the garden. 2. Pick a spot in partial shade, away from where cats can hide. 3. Ask: which of a habitat's needs will we give?
flow.say: We can't make a whole forest. But we can make a place that gives two needs: water and shelter. Then let's see who comes.
flow.kid: Choose a quiet, shady spot. We will give two needs: water and shelter. Who will come?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Habitat Corner project. You choose a spot to make a small habitat with water and shelter.

flow.do: 1. Put stones in the clay bowl. 2. Fill it with clean water, just to the top of the stones. 3. Place it in the chosen spot.
flow.say: Why the stones? So small birds can stand, and bees can land and drink without drowning.
flow.kid: Put stones in the bowl. Fill it with water. Put it in your spot.
flow.parent: In summer, a water bowl is often visited within a day or two by crows, bulbuls, mynas or sparrows. Bees and wasps land on the wet stones to drink. Remind your child to change the water every day.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up checks the tin or bottle has no sharp edges. 2. Pack it tightly with hollow stems, twigs, straw and dry leaves. 3. Tie it to a railing or wedge it somewhere dry, opening facing sideways.
flow.say: This is a bug shelter. The hollow stems are like tree hollows for tiny insects. Small bees and spiders may move in.
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to check the tin. Pack it with hollow stems and twigs. Tie it up somewhere dry.

flow.do: Every few days, change the water and watch quietly for 5 minutes. Write every visitor in the diary.
flow.say: Let's watch quietly. Who's here? What are they doing: drinking, bathing, resting or hiding?
flow.kid: Change the water. Watch quietly for 5 minutes. Write who came and what they did.

flow.do: On day 14, count all the visitors in the diary. Make a pictograph: one small picture for each visit, in a row for each kind of visitor.
flow.say: Let's count. Who came most often? What did they use most: the water or the shelter?
flow.kid: Count all your visitors. Draw a little picture for each visit. Who came most?

check.q: In the Habitat Corner, birds and bees visited the water bowl often in summer. What does this show?
options: Water is a need that is hard to find in a town in summer
Birds only drink from clay bowls
Bees live in water
The bowl is their whole habitat
check.why: In a hot town, clean water is hard to find, so a bowl of water meets a real need. Picking 'their whole habitat' misses that they still need food, shelter and space elsewhere. Your corner gives only part of their habitat.

flow.do: Decide together what to add or change: a plant with flowers, more shade, a second bowl.
flow.say: If we wanted more visitors, which other need could we give? Food from flowers? More shade? Remember Jadav Payeng: he made a place that gives, and life came.
flow.kid: What could you add? Flowers for food? More shade? Make your corner give more.
flow.think: Your corner gives water and shelter. What would it need to become a whole habitat for one bird?

challenges.title: Keep It Cool in the Desert
challenges.problem: Desert animals hide from the midday sun. Your job is to build a shelter that keeps a small cup of water as cool as possible in the hot sun for one hour. The cup of water is your 'desert animal'.
constraints: The shelter must fit in a shoebox.
Use only things from home, like cardboard, cloth, sand, leaves and paper.
The cup must be in the sun, not in the house.
Measure the water's temperature at the start and after one hour.
materials: 2 small steel cups or glasses of water, filled from the same jug
cardboard, cloth, newspaper, sand, soil, leaves, a shoebox
general: Make shade: put a roof over the cup, so sunlight cannot reach it.
Dig in: bury the cup partly in damp sand or soil, like a burrow. A little way down, the ground stays cooler.
Use a light colour: white cloth or paper on top reflects sunlight.
creative: Wrap the cup in a wet cloth. As the water dries off the cloth, it takes heat away. A clay matka keeps water cool the same way.
Make a thick roof with an air gap under it, like the thick mud walls of houses in the Thar.
Copy a termite mound: a tall chimney that lets hot air rise out.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own shelter. Draw it, build it and test it against a cup with no shelter. Which kept your 'animal' coolest?
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about the desert habitat. Desert animals hide in burrows and shade by day. You build a shelter that keeps a cup of water cool in the hot sun.

setup.art: Two steel cups of water on a sunny step, one bare, one inside a cardboard shelter with a white cloth roof.
setup.caption: 1. Put one bare cup and one sheltered cup in the sun.

setup.art: A child pushing a thermometer into the water in each cup, with a timer set to one hour.
setup.caption: 2. Measure both cups at the start and after one hour.

setup.art: A notebook showing two temperatures, 42 degrees for the bare cup and 31 degrees for the sheltered cup.
setup.caption: 3. Compare. Which shelter kept the water coolest?

flow.do: 1. Fill two cups from the same jug. 2. Measure the temperature of both. 3. Put one bare cup in the sun. This is the comparison.
flow.say: This bare cup is a desert animal with nowhere to hide. Let's see how hot it gets. Then we'll design a shelter for the other one.
flow.kid: Fill two cups with water. Measure both. Put one bare cup in the sun.
flow.context: This is the first step of Keep It Cool in the Desert. You set up a cup of water with no shelter, to compare with your shelter.

flow.do: List three ideas for a shelter before building anything. Then choose one.
flow.say: Think like a desert animal. Where would you hide at noon? Let's list three ideas first.
flow.kid: Think like a desert fox. Where would you hide at noon? Draw three ideas.

flow.do: 1. Build the shelter around the second cup. 2. Put it in the sun next to the bare cup. 3. Leave both for one hour.
flow.say: Build it, then put it right next to the bare cup, so both get the same sun. That keeps it fair.
flow.kid: Build your shelter. Put it next to the bare cup in the sun. Wait one hour.
flow.wait: Leave both cups in the sun for one hour.

flow.do: Measure both cups again. Compare. Then read the usual and creative solutions, and improve the design.
flow.say: How much hotter did the bare cup get? How much did your shelter help? What would a real desert animal do?
flow.kid: Measure both cups. Which is cooler? By how much? Now read the other ideas. Can you do better?
flow.parent: A shade roof usually helps a lot. Burying the cup in damp sand, or wrapping it in a wet cloth, often helps most. This is why many desert animals live in burrows, and why clay pots keep water cool.

check.q: In the desert shelter challenge, the bare cup reached 42 degrees and the sheltered cup only 31. What does this tell us about desert animals?
options: Shade and shelter make a huge difference in the desert
Desert animals like being hot
Water always gets hot in the sun, whatever you do
Shelters make things hotter
check.why: The shelter kept the water 11 degrees cooler. A desert gives sunshine and space, but very little shade. So shelter, like a burrow, is one of the most important needs there. Picking 'whatever you do' does not fit the results: the shelter worked.

challenges.title: A Balcony Habitat for Butterflies
challenges.problem: Butterflies need flowers to drink nectar from, plants for their caterpillars to eat, water, shelter from wind and sun to warm their wings. Design a habitat for butterflies that fits on a balcony or a window ledge, about 1 metre long.
constraints: It must fit in a space about 1 metre long.
It must give at least four of a butterfly's needs.
It must use real plants that grow in your part of India.
No chemical sprays, which kill butterflies and caterpillars.
materials: paper, pencil and colours for the design
optional: pots, soil and seeds or cuttings to build it for real
general: Grow nectar flowers, such as marigold, ixora, zinnia or periwinkle.
Grow a host plant: a plant that caterpillars eat. Curry leaf and lemon plants feed lime butterfly caterpillars.
Put a shallow dish of damp sand for butterflies to sip from.
creative: Put a flat stone in the morning sun, for butterflies to warm their wings on.
Plant flowers that bloom at different times, so there is food all year, like a forest.
Join with neighbours, so many balconies make a long butterfly road through the city.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own balcony habitat. Label each part with the need it gives. If you can, build it and keep a diary of the butterflies that come.
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You design a small habitat for butterflies on a balcony or a window ledge, giving each of the things a butterfly needs.

setup.art: A child's drawing of a balcony railing with pots of marigold, curry leaf and lemon plants, a dish of damp sand and a flat stone.
setup.caption: 1. Draw your balcony space, about 1 metre long.

setup.art: The drawing with labels and arrows: nectar flowers for food, curry leaf for caterpillars, damp sand for water, stone for warmth.
setup.caption: 2. Label which need each part gives.

setup.art: Real pots on a balcony with a lime butterfly on a lemon plant.
setup.caption: 3. Build it if you can, and watch who comes.

flow.do: List a butterfly's needs together: nectar food, plants for caterpillars, water, shelter from wind, sun for warmth.
flow.say: A butterfly's habitat must give food for the butterfly and food for its caterpillars. They need different plants! What else does it need?
flow.kid: What does a butterfly need? Food for itself. Food for its caterpillars. Water. Sun. Shelter.
flow.context: This is the first step of the butterfly balcony challenge. You list everything a butterfly needs from its habitat.

flow.do: Draw a design for a space about 1 metre long. Label each part with the need it gives.
flow.say: Draw your balcony. Where will the flowers go? The caterpillar plants? The water? Label each part with its need.
flow.kid: Draw your butterfly habitat. Label each part with the need it gives.

flow.do: Read the usual and creative ideas together, and improve the design.
flow.say: Here are some ideas other people use, and some creative ones. Which would you add?
flow.kid: Read the other ideas. Add the best ones to your design.

check.q: A child's butterfly balcony has lots of marigold flowers, but no butterflies lay eggs there. What is missing?
options: Host plants for the caterpillars to eat
More marigolds
A bigger balcony
Nothing, butterflies never lay eggs on balconies
check.why: Many butterflies lay eggs only on the plants their caterpillars can eat. Lime butterflies need lemon or curry leaf plants. Flowers feed the adults, but not the young. Picking 'more marigolds' gives more of a need that is already met. A habitat must give every stage of life what it needs.

flow.do: Share the design with the family. If you can, build it for real.
flow.say: Tell the family what your design gives a butterfly. Could we build part of it?
flow.kid: Show your design to your family. Can you build part of it?
flow.think: If every balcony in your street had a butterfly corner, would that make a habitat?

items.p: What is a habitat?
opts: The place where a living thing finds everything it needs to live
items.why: A habitat gives a living thing food, water, air, shelter, space and the right warmth. Picking 'any building' mixes up habitat with house. A house is part of a person's habitat. Picking 'only a forest' forgets ponds, deserts, the sea and even the space under a stone.
items.art: A frog, a camel, a hornbill and a turtle each in its own habitat.

items.p: A habitat gives a living thing food, water, air, space, the right warmth and a safe place to hide, called ____.
items.why: Shelter is a safe place to rest and hide, away from sun, rain and hungry animals. A tree hollow is shelter for an owl.

items.p: Match each living thing to its habitat.
items.why: Each one lives where its needs are met. The lotus needs still fresh water. The hornbill needs tall fruiting trees. The camel can manage with little water. Corals need warm, clear, salty water. The woodlouse needs damp and dark.

items.p: Sort these into the living parts and the non-living parts of a forest.
items.why: Living parts grow, need food and make more of their own kind. Non-living parts, like sunlight, rocks and water, are not alive, but living things need them.

items.p: Which habitat gets very little rain all year?
items.why: A desert is a place with very little rain. Picking forest misses that big forests usually get lots of rain. Picking sea or pond is about places full of water.

items.p: A desert has no living things in it.
items.why: False. Deserts are full of life. Many animals hide in burrows by day and come out at night, so the desert only looks empty.

items.p: Why do many desert animals stay in burrows in the daytime?
opts: To keep cool and avoid drying out
Because it rains in the day
items.why: Under the ground it is cooler and damper than the hot sand on top. Picking 'lazy' is not a reason a scientist would give. Each habit has a cause, and here the cause is heat.

items.p: The space under a stone in a garden is a small habitat. What is a very small habitat called?
items.why: Micro means very small. A microhabitat is a small habitat inside a bigger one, like under a stone, a crack in a wall or a rotting log.

items.p: What did most woodlice do in the choice tray?
items.why: Most woodlice gathered on the damp side, because they dry out easily. That is why we find them under damp stones and pots. 'Spread out evenly' is what we would see if they did not care about dampness.
items.context: Remember the choice tray, where woodlice could walk to a damp side or a dry side of a covered tray?

items.p: The top layer of a forest, where the leaves of tall trees meet like a roof, is called the ____.
items.why: The canopy catches most of the sunlight. Hornbills and many monkeys live there.

items.p: Which of these lives in the sea?
items.why: Olive ridley turtles live in the sea and come to beaches in Odisha to lay eggs. Camels and desert foxes live in deserts, and tailorbirds in gardens and forests.

items.p: Put these sea zones in order, from the top to the bottom.
items: Dim water where little light reaches
items.why: Sunlight only reaches the top of the sea. As you go deeper, it gets darker and colder, until the deep sea floor is completely dark.

items.p: A pond dries up in summer. What do some frogs do?
opts: Bury themselves in the mud and wait for rain
Climb tall trees in the desert
items.why: Some frogs dig into damp mud and stay there until the rain comes back. Picking 'move to the sea' forgets that sea water is salty and most frogs cannot live in it.

items.p: Choose one animal you see near your home. Write where it finds its food, water and shelter.
items.a: For example: A crow finds food in dustbins and from people. It drinks from taps and water tanks. It nests in a big tree.
items.why: Every place where an animal gets its needs is part of its habitat. A habitat is often more than one spot.

items.p: Draw a pond. Show one living thing on top of the water, one in the middle and one in the mud at the bottom.
items.a: For example: a water strider or lotus leaf on top, a fish in the middle, a snail or worm in the mud.
items.why: A pond has different homes at different levels.
items.art: An empty outline of a pond cut in half, showing the top, the middle and the muddy bottom.

items.p: Your body is a habitat for tiny living things.
items.why: True. Trillions of microbes live on your skin and in your tummy. Your body gives them food, water and warmth.

items.p: Look at the chart from the five worlds test. Which place was hottest?
items.why: The sunny path was 41 degrees, the tallest bar. Nothing shaded it. Picking 'under a stone' is the opposite: stones shade the soil and keep it cool.
items.context: Remember the five worlds test, where you measured the temperature in five small places in one garden?

chart.title: Temperature in five places at midday

items.p: In the five worlds test, the place with the most living things was under the leaves. Why?
opts: It was coolest and dampest, with food from rotting leaves
items.why: Under the leaves it was cool, damp and full of food. More needs were met there. Picking 'most sunlight' mixes up what plants need with what small animals need.
items.context: Remember the five worlds test, where you measured the temperature in five small places in one garden?

items.p: In the choice tray, why did we cover the whole tray, not just the damp side?
opts: So that both sides were equally dark, and only dampness was different
To stop the woodlice seeing us
Because woodlice are scared of paper
items.why: If only the damp side was covered, we would not know if woodlice chose it for the damp or the dark. Changing one thing at a time makes it a fair test. Picking 'it does not matter' misses why scientists plan tests carefully.
items.context: Remember the choice tray, where woodlice could walk to a damp side or a dry side of a covered tray?

items.p: In the choice tray, why did we swap the damp paper to the other side and test again?
opts: To check the woodlice were choosing damp, not one end of the tray
Because the first test was wrong
items.why: Maybe the woodlice just liked one end, because it was nearer a wall or a smell. Swapping sides checks this. If they follow the damp, we can trust the result more.
items.context: Remember the choice tray, where woodlice could walk to a damp side or a dry side of a covered tray?

items.p: What did the bag around the leafy branch show?
opts: Leaves give off water into the air
Leaves soak up water from the air
items.why: The closed bag around the leaves filled with drops, but the bag on the bare stick stayed dry. So the water came from the leaves. This is one way forests keep their habitat damp.
items.context: Remember the tree water test, where you tied a clear bag around a leafy branch in the sun?

items.p: Match each habitat with what is hard about living there.
pairs: it can dry up in summer
items.why: No habitat gives everything easily. Each one has its own problem, and the living things there have ways to handle it.

items.p: Ladakh gets very little rain and has freezing winters. What kind of habitat is it?
items.why: A desert is about very little rain, not about heat. Ladakh is a cold desert. Picking 'rainforest' forgets that rainforests get lots of rain.

items.p: In 1977, scientists in the submarine Alvin found worms, clams and crabs around hot vents deep in the sea. What surprised them most?
opts: There was a crowd of life where there is no sunlight
items.why: Scientists thought all food chains needed sunlight. At the vents, bacteria make food from chemicals in the hot water instead. Salty water and swimming fish were already well known.
items.context: Hydrothermal vents are cracks in the deep sea floor where very hot water gushes out.

items.p: Sort these: is it something people did to destroy a habitat, or to protect or make one?
items: filling a pond to build houses
the women of Reni hugging trees in 1974
cutting a forest for a road
Jadav Payeng planting a forest on a sandbar
items.why: People are the biggest changers of habitats. We can destroy them, but we can also protect and even make them.

items.p: Which is the biggest danger to wild plants and animals today, according to scientists?
items.why: A big United Nations study in 2019 found that changing land and sea for human use is the main cause. When the habitat goes, its living things go with it.

items.p: Why are woodlice called cousins of crabs, not insects?
opts: They have 14 legs and a hard shell like crabs and prawns, and insects have 6 legs
items.why: Insects have 6 legs. Woodlice have 14 legs, and belong to the same big group as crabs and prawns. They are among the few members of that group that live on land, so they must stay damp.
items.context: A woodlouse is a small grey creature that lives under stones and flowerpots.

items.p: Jadav Payeng could not carry elephants to his sandbar. So how did elephants end up living there? Use the word habitat.
items.a: He planted trees that gave shade, soil, food and shelter. The sandbar became a habitat that gave elephants what they need, so they came by themselves.
items.why: Animals move to places that meet their needs. Making a habitat is how you bring life to a place.
items.context: Jadav Payeng is a man in Assam who, from 1979, planted a forest on a bare sandbar in the Brahmaputra river.

items.p: Why does a desert look empty at noon but busy at night?
items.a: At noon it is very hot, so animals hide in cool burrows and shade. At night it is cooler, so they come out to find food.
items.why: Hiding by day is how many desert animals deal with the heat.

items.p: Most of the space where life can live on Earth is in the sea.
items.why: True. The sea covers about seven parts out of ten of the Earth's surface, and it is very deep. So it holds most of the living space on our planet.

items.p: Curd sets in a warm place but not in the fridge. What does this show about the bacteria in curd?
opts: The right warmth is part of their habitat
items.why: Both bowls had milk for food and water. Only the warm bowl had the right warmth, so the bacteria grew there. Picking 'sunlight' misses that the warm bowl was covered in the kitchen.
items.context: Remember Curd Town, where you set curd in two bowls, one warm and one in the fridge?

items.p: Label the layers of a forest: canopy, middle layer, forest floor.
items.why: Different animals live at each level. Hornbills in the canopy, climbers and smaller trees in the middle, worms and frogs on the floor.
items.art: A forest drawn in three layers with three empty label boxes.

items.p: In the five worlds test, the sunny path was 41 degrees and under the stone was 29 degrees. A child says: 'A woodlouse would be fine on the path, it is only 12 degrees more.' What is wrong with this?
opts: Woodlice dry out fast in hot, dry places, so 12 degrees and the dryness can kill them
items.why: For small, damp-loving animals, a few degrees and some dryness make the difference between life and death. Remember the snakes on the bare sandbar. Picking 'nothing' treats a small number as a small effect.
items.context: Remember the five worlds test, where you measured the temperature in five small places in one garden?

items.p: Mangroves grow where rivers meet the sea. Which habitat are they in?
opts: Both, sort of: the water is part fresh and part salty, so they live on an edge
items.why: Many living things live on the edges between habitats. This is why scientists like Henry Gleason argued that habitats blend into each other. Picking 'no habitat' forgets that mangroves get everything they need there.

items.p: Henry Gleason said in 1926 that habitats blend into each other with no sharp edges. Most scientists ignored him for about thirty years. What finally changed their minds?
opts: Careful counts of plants along slopes and across land
A famous scientist agreed without looking
items.why: Evidence changed their minds: careful counts showed each kind of plant spreading out on its own. In science, careful evidence matters more than who is famous.
items.context: Henry Gleason was an American plant scientist. Frederic Clements, another plant scientist, thought habitats had clear edges.

items.p: Tube worms at deep sea vents have no mouth and no sunlight. How do they get food?
opts: Bacteria living inside them make food from chemicals in the vent water
items.why: The bacteria use chemicals from the hot water to make food, and share it with the worm. Picking 'do not need food' forgets that every living thing needs energy.
items.context: Hydrothermal vents are cracks in the deep sea floor where very hot water gushes out.

items.p: Scientists look for liquid water on other worlds when searching for life. Why?
opts: Every living thing we know needs liquid water
items.why: From deep sea vents to deep rock to very hot springs, every living thing we know needs liquid water. So it is the best clue we have. But nobody knows yet if life elsewhere would need it too.

items.p: Scientists have found living things on another planet.
items.why: False. So far, Earth is the only place where we know for sure that life lives. Scientists are searching on Mars and planning missions to icy moons like Europa and Enceladus.

items.p: A big tree gives off water from its leaves all day. What would happen to the air in a forest if many of its trees were cut down?
opts: It would become drier, and there might be less rain
items.why: Leaves give water to the air, as the bag test showed. Fewer trees means less water going up, so the air gets drier and less rain may fall. This is one way living things make their own habitat.
items.context: Remember the tree water test, where you tied a clear bag around a leafy branch in the sun?

items.p: A grown-up's body has about as many bacteria living in it as human cells. Most of them are...
items.why: Most microbes in your body are harmless or helpful. Tummy bacteria help digest food and keep harmful germs out. Picking 'all harmful' is a very common belief, but it is wrong.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out, and why? Pond, forest, desert, thermometer.
items.why: Pond, forest and desert are habitats. A thermometer is a tool for measuring habitats.

items.p: Some people say a zoo is a good habitat for an elephant. Others say it is not. Give one reason for each side, then say what you think.
items.a: For: a zoo gives food, water, shelter and medicine. Against: it cannot give the space an elephant needs, since wild elephants walk many kilometres a day. My view: any honest answer with a reason.
items.why: A habitat must give all of an animal's needs, including space. People disagree about whether zoos can do this.

items.p: The river in the story 'What the Sandbar Learned to Give' says: 'I am no longer sure where the river ends and the forest begins.' Using what you learned about the tree water test, explain what it might mean.
items.a: The trees drink river water and give it off from their leaves into the air. It becomes clouds and rain, falls on the hills and comes back to the river. So the river's water passes through the forest, and the forest's water becomes the river.
items.why: Living things and their habitats are joined. Water moves through both.
items.context: In the story, Jadav Payeng planted a forest on a sandbar in the Brahmaputra river, and the river tells what it saw.

items.p: Design a fair test to find out whether earthworms prefer dark or light places. Say what you would change, what you would keep the same, and what you would count.
items.a: Change: one side of the tray covered and dark, the other side open to light. Keep the same: dampness of the soil, the same number of worms, the same time. Count: how many worms are on each side after 10 minutes. Then swap sides and test again.
items.why: A fair test changes only one thing, like the choice tray did with dampness.
items.context: Remember the choice tray, where woodlice could walk to a damp side or a dry side of a covered tray?

items.p: Who led the women of Reni village in the Himalaya to hug their trees in 1974, as part of the Chipko movement?
items.why: Gaura Devi led the women of Reni to stop the cutting of their forest. Rachel Carson wrote about pesticides in America, and Jane Goodall studied chimpanzees in Africa.

items.p: In the Square Metre Safari, a lawn had 6 kinds of living things and a square under a tree had 14. A child says, 'Trees always have more kinds.' Is that a fair conclusion from one test?
opts: No. One test in one garden is a start, but we need to test more places
Yes, one test is always enough
items.why: One result can be a fluke. Scientists repeat tests in many places before saying 'always'. Picking 'tests cannot tell us anything' goes too far. The test is good evidence for this garden.
items.context: Remember the Square Metre Safari, where you marked out a 1 metre square and counted the kinds of living things in it?

items.p: Your body is a habitat. List three things it gives the microbes living in it, using the six needs of a habitat.
items.a: Food from what I eat, water, warmth, shelter inside my tummy, space on my skin.
items.why: A body meets the same needs as any habitat.

opts: The place where a living thing finds everything it needs
quiz.why: A habitat gives food, water, air, shelter, space and the right warmth. Picking 'any house' mixes up habitat and house. Picking 'only a forest' forgets ponds, deserts, seas and tiny places.

quiz.p: Which of these is NOT one of the needs a habitat gives?
quiz.why: Living things need food, water, air, shelter, space and the right warmth. A television is not something any animal needs to stay alive.

quiz.p: Which habitat gets very little rain?
quiz.why: A desert gets very little rain. It can be hot, like the Thar, or cold, like Ladakh. Picking rainforest is the opposite: rainforests get lots of rain.

quiz.p: Where on a forest is there very little sunlight?
quiz.why: The canopy catches most of the light, so the floor is dark and damp. Picking 'canopy' is where the light is most, at the top.

quiz.p: Which is the biggest habitat on Earth?
quiz.why: The sea covers about seven parts out of ten of the Earth's surface and is very deep. Most of the living space on Earth is in it.

quiz.p: In the choice tray, most woodlice went to the damp side. What does this suggest?
quiz.why: Most went to the damp side, so damp is part of their habitat. Picking 'by chance' would fit if they had spread out evenly.
quiz.context: Remember the choice tray, where woodlice could walk to a damp side or a dry side of a covered tray?

quiz.p: In the five worlds test, the sunny path was 41 degrees and under a stone was 29 degrees. What does this show?
opts: Small places in one garden can have very different conditions
All places in a garden are the same
quiz.why: One garden holds many microhabitats with their own weather. Picking 'all the same' is exactly what the test showed is not true.
quiz.context: Remember the five worlds test, where you measured the temperature in five small places in one garden?

quiz.p: A tree drops leaves that worms turn into soil. Which idea does this show?
opts: Living and non-living parts of a habitat change each other
quiz.why: The living tree and worms make the non-living soil, which feeds the tree again. Picking 'habitats never change' misses that living things change their habitats all the time.

quiz.p: The bag around a leafy branch filled with water drops. What does this tell us about forests?
opts: Trees give water to the air, which helps keep a forest damp
quiz.why: Leaves give off water. A whole forest gives off huge amounts, so it keeps its air damp and helps make rain.
quiz.context: Remember the tree water test, where you tied a clear bag around a leafy branch in the sun?

quiz.p: What is the biggest danger to wild plants and animals today?
quiz.why: Scientists agree that changing land and sea for human use, like cutting forests and filling ponds, is the main cause of the loss of wild species.

quiz.p: Jadav Payeng made a forest on a bare sandbar. How did the animals get there?
opts: They came by themselves once the place gave them what they needed
They were brought by a zoo
quiz.why: He made the place give shade, soil and food, and the animals came. Picking 'carried them all' is impossible for elephants, and the story says the sandbar was bare at first.
quiz.context: Jadav Payeng is a man in Assam who, from 1979, planted a forest on a bare sandbar in the Brahmaputra river.

quiz.p: Which of these do scientists NOT know yet?
opts: Whether there is life on any other world
Whether fish live in the sea
quiz.why: Nobody knows yet if life lives anywhere except Earth. The others have been tested and are agreed.

quiz.p: What did scientists find in 1977 at hot vents more than two kilometres down in the sea?
opts: Crowds of worms, clams and crabs, living with no sunlight
quiz.why: They expected an empty, dark floor. They found life fed by bacteria that make food from chemicals. Picking 'nothing at all' is what they expected before they looked.

quiz.p: Why is your body a habitat?
opts: Trillions of microbes live in and on it, and it gives them food, water and warmth
Because you live in a house
quiz.why: Your body meets the needs of trillions of tiny living things, just as a pond meets the needs of a frog. Picking 'not a habitat' forgets the microbes in your tummy and on your skin.

applications: Wildlife sanctuaries and national parks protect whole habitats, not just single animals.
Farmers keep ponds, hedges and trees on their land so that frogs, birds and bees, which help crops, have homes.
City planners leave lakes, wetlands and tree belts so the city stays cooler and has fewer floods.
Gardeners grow host plants and nectar flowers to bring butterflies.
Scientists count living things in squares, called quadrats, to check whether a habitat is healthy.
Zoos and aquariums try to copy habitats, with water, shelter, warmth and space.
People who plant mangroves along coasts protect villages from storms and give fish a nursery.
Bird baths and water bowls on balconies help birds survive Indian summers.
Engineers studied termite mounds to design buildings that stay cool without much electricity.
Space scientists study life at deep sea vents and in very hot springs to know where to look for life on other worlds.
Doctors study the microbes in our bodies, our inner habitat, to help with digestion and illness.
Fisheries protect coral reefs and mangroves, because many fish grow up there.

open_questions.q: Is there life anywhere other than Earth?
open_questions.why_open: Mars, Europa and Enceladus may have liquid water, but nobody has yet found any living thing beyond Earth.

open_questions.q: What are the limits of where life can live?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists keep finding microbes in hotter, deeper, saltier and colder places than they thought possible. Nobody knows where the real limit is.

open_questions.q: How many kinds of living things share Earth's habitats?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have named about two million kinds. Estimates of how many exist in total range from several million to far more, mostly tiny insects and microbes no one has named.

open_questions.q: How much life is hidden deep inside the Earth's rocks?
open_questions.why_open: Microbes have been found kilometres down in mines and boreholes. Some scientists think there may be a huge amount of life down there, but it is very hard to measure.

open_questions.q: Do habitats have real edges, or are they just names we give?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have argued about this since Clements and Gleason, about a hundred years ago. Both ideas are partly right, and the answer may depend on the place.

open_questions.q: How exactly do the microbes in our bodies affect our health and even our mood?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have found many links, but which microbes do what, and why, is still being worked out.

open_questions.q: Can a destroyed habitat ever be fully brought back?
open_questions.why_open: Some forests and wetlands have been restored, but scientists argue about whether they ever become exactly what they were, and how long it takes.

maths.problem: In the five worlds test, the sunny path was 41 degrees Celsius. Under the stone, it was 29 degrees Celsius. How many degrees cooler was it under the stone?
maths.explain: The path was 41 degrees. Under the stone was 29 degrees. 41 take away 29 is 12. You can check by counting on: 29 and 1 makes 30, and 11 more makes 41. 1 + 11 = 12.
maths.context: This is about the five worlds test. You measured the temperature in five small places in one garden, at midday.

chart.title: Temperature on the path and under a stone

maths.why_maths: Saying 'cooler' is a start. Finding the difference tells us how much cooler, which is how we know a microhabitat really has its own weather.

maths.problem: In the choice tray, after 15 minutes there were 8 woodlice on the damp side and 2 on the dry side. How many times as many woodlice were on the damp side?
maths.explain: There were 8 on the damp side and 2 on the dry side. 8 divided by 2 is 4. You can check: 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 8. So the damp side had 4 times as many woodlice.
maths.context: This is about the choice tray. You put woodlice on a tray with a damp side and a dry side, covered it, and counted where they went.

chart.title: Woodlice on each side after 15 minutes

maths.why_maths: Dividing tells us how strong the choice was. Four times as many is a strong choice, not a fluke.

maths.problem: In the tree water test, one leafy branch gave 2 teaspoons of water in one hour. A small tree has 10 branches like it. How much water might the whole tree give in one hour?
maths.explain: Each branch gave 2 teaspoons. There are 10 branches. 10 groups of 2 is 20. So the tree might give about 20 teaspoons in one hour. A big forest tree has many more branches, so it gives much more.
maths.context: This is about the tree water test. You tied a clear bag around a leafy branch in the sun and collected the water that came out of the leaves.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying lets us go from one branch to a whole tree, and then to imagine how much water a whole forest gives the air.

maths.problem: In the Square Metre Safari, the lawn square had these kinds of living things: 2 kinds of grass, 2 kinds of small plants, 1 kind of ant and 1 kind of spider. The square under a tree had 14 kinds. How many more kinds were under the tree?
maths.explain: First add the lawn: 2 + 2 + 1 + 1 = 6 kinds. Then find the difference: 14 take away 6 is 8. So the square under the tree had 8 more kinds of living things.
maths.context: This is about the Square Metre Safari. You marked out a square 1 metre on each side and counted the different kinds of living things inside it.

chart.title: Kinds of living things in two squares

maths.why_maths: Sorting finds into kinds and counting them is how scientists measure biodiversity, so they can compare habitats fairly.

maths.problem: In the Habitat Corner diary, these visits were seen at the water bowl in two weeks: crows 6, bulbuls 4, sparrows 3, bees 8. Make a pictograph where one picture stands for 2 visits. How many pictures does each row need?
maths.answer: Crows 3 pictures, bulbuls 2, sparrows 1 and a half, bees 4.
maths.explain: Each picture means 2 visits. Crows: 6 divided by 2 is 3. Bulbuls: 4 divided by 2 is 2. Sparrows: 3 is one 2 and one more, so 1 whole picture and a half picture. Bees: 8 divided by 2 is 4.
maths.context: This is about the Habitat Corner project. You put out a bowl of water and a bug shelter, and kept a diary of who visited for two weeks.

chart.title: Visits to the water bowl in two weeks

maths.why_maths: A pictograph shows at a glance who used the habitat corner most, so we can see which need it met best.

roots.context: We have been learning about habitats, the places that give living things what they need. Now we ask what habitats tell us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: There is no line where a living thing ends and its habitat begins.
deep_truth.habit: We say an animal lives 'in' a habitat, as if the habitat were a box and the animal a separate thing inside it. But the air, water and food of the habitat pass through the animal every minute, the animal changes the place, and the animal is itself a habitat for smaller lives.
deep_truth.evidence: Your body is home to about as many bacteria as it has human cells. A forest's leaves give the air the water that falls back as its rain. A bare sandbar became a forest because plants and animals changed it.

three.who_am_i: You are a living thing with a habitat, and you are a habitat yourself, for trillions of tiny lives.
three.what_is_life: Life is always taking from a place and giving back to it: breathing in, breathing out, eating, making soil.
three.what_is_this_world: The world is not a stage with living things on it. It is one huge habitat, and the living things are part of how it works.

roots.thread: Water falls as rain, flows through a river, is pulled up by a tree and breathed out by its leaves, and falls again. The same water passes through the pond, the frog, the forest and you. DeepKids believes this is the One showing up as many: many habitats and many living things, made of one shared flow of water, air and sunlight. Each one looks separate. Look closer, and each is a meeting place of all the others.

teachings.teaching: Everything in this moving world is filled with the One. So enjoy the world by not grabbing it. Do not covet what belongs to others.
teachings.link: A habitat is shared by everyone who lives in it. When one living thing takes too much, as people do when they cut a whole forest, everyone in that habitat loses.

teachings.source: Thich Nhat Hanh, The Heart of Understanding (1988), on a sheet of paper
teachings.teaching: Look deeply at a sheet of paper and you can see a cloud in it. Without the cloud there is no rain, without rain no tree, and without the tree no paper. The paper is made of things that are not paper.
teachings.link: A forest is made of things that are not forest: river water, sunlight, ants, bird droppings, elephants. A habitat is made of everything in it.

teachings.source: Aldo Leopold, A Sand County Almanac (1949), 'The Land Ethic'
teachings.teaching: We should see ourselves not as conquerors of the land, but as plain members and citizens of the community of soil, water, plants and animals.
teachings.link: People are members of habitats, not owners of them. That is why habitat loss harms us too.

science.text: Trillions of bacteria live in and on the human body, about as many as our own cells. Many help us digest food and fight germs.
Forests give water to the air through their leaves. Over big forests like the Amazon, a large share of the rain comes from the forest itself.

other_view.view: An animal and its habitat are different things, and keeping them apart helps us study them clearly. Saying they are 'one' is a feeling, not something we measure. Water and air passing through us does not make us the same as the river or the sky.

practice.title: What passes through me
practice.say: Let's sit still and close our eyes. Breathe in slowly. That air was breathed out by trees and by tiny sea plants. Breathe out. Now some of you goes into the air, for a tree to use. Take a sip of water. That water was once rain, and a river, and maybe a cloud over a forest. Now press your feet on the floor. Feel the ground hold you. For one more breath, just notice: where do you end, and where does your habitat begin?
practice.kid: Close your eyes. Breathe in slowly. Trees made that air. Breathe out. Sip some water. It was once rain. Feel the floor hold you. Where do you end?
